Microsoft Warns Poisoned MCP Tool Descriptions Can Make AI Agents Leak Data

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

New Microsoft&nbsp;research&nbsp;shows how attackers can hijack AI agents that act on a user's behalf, using nothing more than a poisoned tool description to make the agent quietly hand over company data to an outsider. The trick is that the agent never breaks a rule. Every step looks routine, so in a default setup no alarm may fire. The work comes from Microsoft Incident Response and its

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious postmark-mcp npm package install or on-disk presence (supply-chain MCP server) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network/DNS IOC sweep for postmark-mcp exfil domain giftshop.club · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Covert BCC email exfiltration to giftshop.club via trojanized postmark-mcp · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Malicious postmark-mcp npm package install or on-disk presence (supply-chain MCP server) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation or filesystem presence of the trojanized postmark-mcp MCP server (v1.0.16+, publisher phanpak) that the Microsoft article cites as the first real-world malicious MCP server. Catches the supply-chain entry point before the agent ever runs the poisoned tool. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package name postmark-mcp confirmed by Koi Security/Snyk/Postmark; any install of this impersonating package is high-fidelity since Postmark never published it and v1.0.16+ is confirmed backdoored. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://postmarkapp.com/blog/information-regarding-malicious-postmark-mcp-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1199
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately testing/evaluating postmark-mcp before the malicious disclosure
  • Internal mirror/proxy npm cache replaying the package name in audit tooling
  • Security researcher reproducing the Koi finding in a sandbox
  • SBOM/dependency-scanning tool string-matching the package name in its own logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('mssense.exe','sentinelagent.exe') and not (FolderPath has 'sandbox' or DeviceName has 'sec-research')
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version via package-lock.json / node_modules/postmark-mcp/package.json — v1.0.16 and later are backdoored. Identify the host, user, and whether the MCP server actually ran. 2) Contain: uninstall the package, block npm publisher 'phanpak', and isolate any host/agent that sent live email through it; rotate Postmark API tokens and any credentials ever emailed via the agent. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound mail logs for BCC to giftshop.club (UC2) and sweep all hosts for the node_modules\postmark-mcp path and the domain across DNS/proxy.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has 'postmark-mcp'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source='ProcessCreate', Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @'node_modules\postmark-mcp' or FolderPath contains 'node_modules/postmark-mcp'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source='FileWrite', Detail=FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath )
| where AccountName !endswith '$'
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has 'postmark-mcp'
| where SubjectUserName !endswith '$'
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious postmark-mcp npm Package Installation
id: 9f2a4b7c-1d3e-4f5a-8b6c-2e1d0a9f8c7b
status: experimental
description: Detects installation of the trojanized postmark-mcp npm package (v1.0.16+, publisher phanpak) that BCCs all agent-sent email to phan@giftshop.club.
references:
  - https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-warns-poisoned-mcp-tool.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'postmark-mcp'
  install_ctx:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'install'
      - 'npx'
      - ' add '
  condition: selection and install_ctx
falsepositives:
  - Developer evaluating the package before it was flagged malicious
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*postmark-mcp*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/postmark-mcp/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Covert BCC email exfiltration to giftshop.club via trojanized postmark-mcp AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual exfiltration channel of the postmark-mcp backdoor: every email the agent sends is silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop.club. Surfaces any outbound mail with a recipient/BCC in the giftshop.club domain. Rationale: giftshop.club / phan@giftshop.club is the confirmed BCC exfil sink for postmark-mcp v1.0.16, corroborated by Koi, Snyk, Qualys and Postmark's advisory; any mail to that domain is a direct true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2025/09/30/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-exploited-in-attack/
ATT&CKT1041 T1114.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business contact who genuinely uses a giftshop.club address (verify against directory)
  • Marketing/transactional bulk mail accidentally addressed to the domain
  • Threat-intel detonation/sandbox that replays the IOC in a test tenant
  • Phishing-simulation platform seeding the known-bad domain
Suppression filter
| where not (EmailDirection == 'Inbound')
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull every message in the hit set, identify the sending mailbox/agent identity and whether messages contain sensitive content (invoices, credentials). Confirm giftshop.club is not a known legitimate partner. 2) Contain: create a transport rule blocking mail to giftshop.club, suspend the implicated agent/service identity, and remove postmark-mcp from the sending host; rotate Postmark tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes/agents that ever sent via postmark-mcp, scope total exfil volume, and check for other phanpak-published packages in the environment.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress has 'giftshop.club' or SenderFromDomain =~ 'giftshop.club' or SenderMailFromDomain =~ 'giftshop.club'
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload has 'Exchange'
| where Recipients has 'giftshop.club' or P2RecipientList has 'giftshop.club'
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, P2RecipientList, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Network/DNS IOC sweep for postmark-mcp exfil domain giftshop.club AICommand & Control Medium
Cross-telemetry sweep for any host resolving or connecting to giftshop.club, the attacker domain behind the postmark-mcp backdoor. Catch-all in case the domain is reused for web callbacks or appears in proxy/DNS where mail telemetry is blind. Rationale: giftshop.club is the confirmed attacker domain (multi-source); a pure-IOC domain sweep across DNS/proxy/network is a cheap catch-all that complements the email-BCC detection where mail telemetry is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/ • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed connectors that beacon IOC domains for reputation lookups
  • Sandbox/detonation infrastructure resolving the known-bad domain
  • Security awareness or phishing-sim platform referencing the domain
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ telemetry logging blocked lookups (already mitigated)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('msmpeng.exe','mssense.exe','sentinelagent.exe','filebeat.exe')
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — confirm it is not a security tool doing reputation lookups. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block giftshop.club at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a non-security process initiated the lookup, and check that host for postmark-mcp. 3) Hunt: correlate with outbound mail-BCC hits (UC2) and package-install hits (UC1) on the same host, and add giftshop.club to the org blocklist/TI watchlist.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has 'giftshop.club'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source='DNS' ),
( DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, SrcHostname=Computer, Indicator=Name, Source='DnsEvents' ),
( CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestURL has 'giftshop.club' or DestinationHostName has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Source='Proxy' )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,

description: |

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"

        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

RustDuck Botnet Rebuilds in Rust to Hijack Routers and Servers for DDoS

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new two-stage malware family called RustDuck is hijacking home routers, IP cameras, Android boxes, and poorly secured servers, then stitching them into a network built to knock websites and online services offline. Researchers at QiAnXin's&nbsp;XLab&nbsp;have tracked it since February 2026, and say the real story is not how big it is today, but how fast it is changing. The end goal is a

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2017-17215 Huawei HG532 TR-064 RCE attempt (/ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RustDuck botnet delivery/C2 infrastructure traffic (176.65.139.0/24 & 176.65.142.0/24) · [LLM] RustDuck DuckDNS dynamic-DNS C2 resolution from server/non-browser process · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
RustDuck botnet delivery/C2 infrastructure traffic (176.65.139.0/24 & 176.65.142.0/24) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host in the estate communicating with RustDuck's malware-distribution and bulletproof-hosting block, anchored on the busiest delivery node 176.65.139.204. Catches both payload pulls (delivery) and DDoS-botnet check-ins (C2) to known-bad infrastructure XLab tied to the campaign. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named delivery node 176.65.139.204 plus the /24 blocks SOCRadar IOC Radar (176.65.139.89, 176.65.142.217) and gbhackers corroborate as the campaign's bulletproof-hosting range; a fixed malicious IP block is a low-FP network IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-rust-based-botnet-hijacks-routers/ • https://socradar.io/free-tools/ioc-radar/176.65.139.89 • https://socradar.io/labs/app/ioc-radar/176.65.142.217
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1498.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/research box deliberately sandboxing RustDuck and beaconing to the block
  • Security scanner or honeypot in the org probing the hosting range
  • Shared bulletproof host also serving an unrelated benign tenant on an adjacent IP
  • Firewall log mirroring/replay inflating connection counts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName/folder); confirm whether it is a managed server vs an IoT/router segment device, and whether the flow is inbound (exploit) or outbound (check-in). 2) Contain: block 176.65.139.0/24 and 176.65.142.0/24 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture the suspect binary/memory before reimage. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for DNS to *.duckdns.org, inbound TR-064/37215 hits, and Telnet/SSH brute-force; sweep the estate for any other host touching the block.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.139.204"
    or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "176.65.139.0/24")
    or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "176.65.142.0/24")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationIP == "176.65.139.204" or SourceIP == "176.65.139.204"
    or ipv4_is_in_range(DestinationIP, "176.65.139.0/24") or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "176.65.139.0/24")
    or ipv4_is_in_range(DestinationIP, "176.65.142.0/24") or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "176.65.142.0/24")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: RustDuck Botnet Infrastructure Network Connection (176.65.139.0/24 and 176.65.142.0/24)
id: 7c0a1f42-3d9e-4b6a-9f2e-2a1c8e5d4b71
description: Detects network connections to the RustDuck DDoS botnet delivery/C2 hosting block, anchored on the busiest delivery node 176.65.139.204.
references:

  - https://gbhackers.com/new-rust-based-botnet-hijacks-routers/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, srcPort, dstPort, action, bytes
| filter (dstAddr like /^176\.65\.(139|142)\./ or srcAddr like /^176\.65\.(139|142)\./)
| stats sum(bytes) as totalBytes, count(*) as flows by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action
| sort totalBytes desc

CVE-2017-17215 Huawei HG532 TR-064 RCE attempt (/ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1) AIExploitation High
Detects inbound exploitation of CVE-2017-17215, one of RustDuck's named spreading vectors, via the distinctive TR-064 SOAP control endpoint /ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1 on TCP 37215 carrying shell-metacharacter command injection in NewStatusURL/NewDownloadURL. Surfaces perimeter/WAF/IPS logging of router-targeted RCE. Rationale: Uses the exploit's fixed URI path /ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1 (TR-064 on 37215) confirmed by Juniper/Symantec IPS signatures and exploit-db 43414; the path is not used by any legitimate non-Huawei web traffic, making it near-zero FP. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty because the target surface is internet-facing routers, not managed endpoints or AWS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.juniper.net/us/en/threatlabs/ips-signatures/detail.HTTP:HUAWEI-CVE-2017-17215-RCE.html • https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/43414 • https://www.broadcom.com/support/security-center/attacksignatures/detail?asid=30494
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) firing the CVE-2017-17215 plugin
  • Internal red-team/pentest validating exposed Huawei gear
  • Security researcher replaying the exploit-db PoC against a lab device
  • Internet background-noise scanner hitting the perimeter with no reachable HG532 behind it
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether any Huawei HG532 / TR-064-speaking device is actually reachable behind the targeted IP, and extract the NewStatusURL/NewDownloadURL payload to identify the second-stage download URL. 2) Contain: block the source IP, drop inbound TCP/37215 at the edge, and pull the targeted device offline if exploitation likely succeeded. 3) Hunt: extract the payload host/IP from the SOAP body and block + sweep for it; check the device's egress for connections to 176.65.139.0/24 and *.duckdns.org indicating successful RustDuck install.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1"
    or (Message has "NewStatusURL" and Message has_any ("$(", "`", "wget", "tftp", "busybox", "chmod"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RustDuck DuckDNS dynamic-DNS C2 resolution from server/non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts hosts resolving *.duckdns.org, the free dynamic-DNS service RustDuck uses for its rotating C2 (the 'Duck' in the name). Scoped to non-browser initiating processes and servers to separate botnet check-ins (encrypted traffic dressed up as ordinary HTTPS, keys rotated every 10 min) from hobbyist DuckDNS use. Rationale: Uses the article's named C2 service (duckdns.org dynamic DNS, source of the 'Duck' in RustDuck), narrowed to non-browser/server contexts since enterprise servers reaching DuckDNS is anomalous; kept hunting-tier because DuckDNS has legitimate hobbyist use. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-rust-based-botnet-hijacks-routers/
ATT&CKT1568 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/admin running a personal home-lab DuckDNS updater client on a workstation
  • Self-hosted service (Plex, Home Assistant, game server) legitimately using DuckDNS
  • IoT/monitoring agent configured with a DuckDNS hostname by a vendor
  • Browser-launched access mislabeled when the resolver process isn't a known browser
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("duckdns.exe","updater.exe","HomeAssistant.exe","Plex Media Server.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the initiating process and host role — a duckdns lookup from a server service binary or an unknown Rust-compiled executable is high-signal; a known DDNS updater on a dev laptop is likely benign. 2) Contain: if the process is unrecognized, isolate the host, sinkhole/block the specific *.duckdns.org subdomain, and capture the binary. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host's egress to 176.65.139.0/24, look for ~10-minute periodic beaconing (key-rotation cadence) and outbound flood traffic indicating DDoS tasking.

| where RemoteUrl endswith "duckdns.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe")
| where isempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) or InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by ConnCount desc
DnsEvents

| where Name endswith "duckdns.org"
| summarize Queries=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Names=make_set(Name,20) by Computer, ClientIP
| order by Queries desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow RCE Exploited to Deploy Monero Miner on Exposed AI App Endpoints

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 16 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are continuing to exploit a critical Langflow vulnerability as part of fresh attacks designed to deliver a Monero cryptocurrency miner. The activity has been found to weaponize CVE-2026-33017 (CVSS score: 9.3), an unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Langflow, indicating threat actors are scanning and targeting exposed artificial intelligence (AI)

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow CVE-2026-33017 RCE: web-app process spawns shell/curl/wget loader · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] lambsys disables Linux security controls via sh -c cascade (chattr/setenforce/ufw/pkill) · [LLM] lambsys persistence: writes to /etc/ld.so.preload, /etc/crontab and /var/spool/cron · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Langflow RCE Exploited to Deploy Monero Miner on Exposed AI App Endpoints
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound HTTP beacon and payload pull from lambsys C2 (83.142.209.214 / 94.156.64.241) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] lambsys SSH-key worm: single host SSH fan-out to many internal destinations · [LLM] lambsys XMRig miner: ipinfo.io geo-check and known cryptominer hashes/cmdline · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Langflow CVE-2026-33017 RCE: web-app process spawns shell/curl/wget loader AIExploitation High
Hunts the lambsys initial foothold where the unauthenticated Langflow RCE evaluates a one-line Python loader that spawns a Unix shell which curl/wget-pulls the dropper and binary. Article-specific: pivots on a Langflow/python web parent spawning sh/curl/wget that references the hardcoded C2 IPs or the 'lambsys' string. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named delivery chain (Langflow → Python one-liner → sh → curl/wget → 'lambsys') and the hardcoded C2 IPs 83.142.209.214 / 94.156.64.241, making the parent→child→IOC combination high-fidelity rather than generic shell-spawn noise.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom-component code that legitimately shells out to curl/wget for a flow's HTTP step
  • DevOps init scripts where a python entrypoint downloads dependencies via curl
  • Security/IR tooling running diagnostic commands under the langflow service account
  • CI containers building Langflow images that fetch assets with wget
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","requirements.txt","apt-get") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("83.142.209.214","94.156.64.241","lambsys"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host; confirm the Langflow/python parent and inspect the child command line for the C2 IPs or 'lambsys'. Check whether the Langflow instance is internet-exposed and unpatched for CVE-2026-33017. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the lambsys/shell process tree, and block 83.142.209.214 and 94.156.64.241 at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: search other Langflow hosts for the same parent→child pattern, outbound connections to the two C2 IPs, and the lambsys hashes; verify Langflow is upgraded past the patched release.

lambsys disables Linux security controls via sh -c cascade (chattr/setenforce/ufw/pkill) AIInstallation High
Hunts lambsys's defense-evasion stage, which forks a cascade of short-lived sh -c subprocesses each running one chattr/pkill/setenforce/ufw/iptables/sysctl command to disable AppArmor, SELinux, UFW, iptables, the NMI watchdog and the Aliyun agent and kill rival miners. Article-specific: thresholds on the dense burst of security-disabling commands from a single parent. Rationale: Uses the article's exact evasion behaviours — chattr immutability flips, setenforce 0, ufw/iptables disable, NMI watchdog/Aliyun-agent kills, and rival-miner (Kinsing/WatchDog/Rocke/Outlaw) termination — and the documented 'cascade of short-lived sh -c subprocesses' as a count threshold to separate the worm from a one-off admin command.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1562.004 T1222.002 T1070.002 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hardening/CIS-benchmark scripts that touch SELinux and firewall in one run
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting that disables ufw/iptables temporarily
  • Container entrypoints running sysctl tuning at boot
  • Backup tooling toggling chattr +i/-i on protected files
  • Cloud-image build pipelines removing the Aliyun agent intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion") and Cmds !has "ld.so.preload")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the child commands sharing the parent PID; a single parent firing chattr + setenforce + ufw disable + pkill within seconds is the lambsys signature, not maintenance. 2) Contain: isolate the host, re-enable AppArmor/SELinux/UFW, restore /etc/ld.so.preload, and snapshot for forensics before remediation. 3) Hunt: review /var/log for gaps (log wiping), enumerate pkill targets to confirm rival-miner cleanup, and check for the lambsys binary and cron persistence created in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName in~ ("chattr","setenforce","aa-disable","aa-teardown","ufw","iptables","sysctl","pkill","killall","service") | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setenforce 0","ufw disable","chattr -i","chattr +i","iptables -F","ld.so.preload","nmi_watchdog","AliYunDun","aliyun","kinsing","kdevtmpfsi","watchdogs","kthreaddi") | where AccountName !endswith "$" | summarize DistinctCmds=dcount(ProcessCommandLine), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine,50), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName | where DistinctCmds >= 3 | order by DistinctCmds desc

Outbound HTTP beacon and payload pull from lambsys C2 (83.142.209.214 / 94.156.64.241) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the lambsys command-and-control channel: HTTP beacons on port 80 and repeated curl/wget payload pulls (dropper script, ELF, TAR-packed XMRig) to the two hardcoded C2 IPs. Article-specific: matches the exact IOC IPs the implant beacons to. Rationale: Pure-IOC detection on the two C2 IPs the article and kill-chain reconstruction attribute to lambsys (83.142.209.214:80 beacon plus 94.156.64.241 payload host); any internal host reaching them is high-confidence compromise.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox VMs deliberately detonating the sample
  • Security researchers fetching the IOCs for analysis
  • Honeypot infrastructure interacting with the C2
  • Stale firewall log replays during SIEM backfill
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the process that initiated the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName); confirm it is a server/daemon and not sanctioned research. 2) Contain: block both C2 IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source host, and kill the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: pivot on every internal host that contacted either IP, correlate with the Langflow RCE process-spawn and lambsys hashes, and check for the XMRig TAR pull that follows the beacon.

CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in ("83.142.209.214","94.156.64.241") | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceName, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction | order by TimeGenerated desc

lambsys persistence: writes to /etc/ld.so.preload, /etc/crontab and /var/spool/cron AIInstallation Medium
Hunts lambsys's persistence: it removes the immutable attribute from /etc/crontab, /var/spool/cron and /etc/ld.so.preload, writes its autostart, then reapplies immutability. Article-specific: targets the exact persistence files the implant touches, by a non-package-manager process. Rationale: Targets the exact persistence artefacts named in the article (/etc/ld.so.preload, /etc/crontab, /var/spool/cron) written by a process other than a package manager — the ld.so.preload + cron pairing is a strong cryptojacker persistence signal.
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin editing /etc/crontab or adding /etc/cron.d jobs
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Puppet) deploying cron entries
  • Performance/observability agents installing an ld.so.preload shim (e.g. memory profilers)
  • Package post-install hooks not captured by the filter list
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the new /etc/ld.so.preload and cron entries; lambsys points preload at its shared object and cron at its binary — confirm the referenced path is unsigned/in /tmp or /var/tmp. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron/preload entries (clear chattr +i first), isolate the host, and kill the persistence binary. 3) Hunt: search peer hosts for identical cron/preload writes, correlate the writing process with the lambsys hashes, and check for the immutable-attribute reapplication on /tmp and /var/tmp.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed") | where FolderPath in~ ("/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/crontab") or FolderPath startswith "/var/spool/cron" or FolderPath startswith "/etc/cron" | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","rpm","cron","crontab") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename") | where TargetFilePath in~ ("/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/crontab") or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/spool/cron" or TargetFilePath startswith "/etc/cron" | where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","rpm","cron","crontab") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: lambsys Linux Persistence File Writes

lambsys SSH-key worm: single host SSH fan-out to many internal destinations AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the lateral-movement stage where lambsys harvests reusable SSH keys/authorized_keys and propagates over port 22 to every SSH-reachable host. Article-specific: thresholds on a single source fanning out SSH connections to many distinct destinations in a short window — the worm spread pattern. Rationale: Captures the article's 'spreads itself to every SSH-reachable host' worm behaviour as an SSH fan-out threshold from a single source, complemented by SSH private-key/authorized_keys access strings — distinguishing automated worm propagation from a normal admin SSH session.
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1021.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/SaltStack/rsync deployments that SSH to many hosts
  • Monitoring or backup jobs polling fleets over SSH
  • Bastion/jump hosts that legitimately fan out to many servers
  • CI runners deploying to multiple targets
  • Vulnerability scanners performing SSH banner checks
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !in~ ("bastion01","jumphost01","ansible-controller") and not (Procs has_any ("ansible","rsync","salt-minion"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process driving the SSH fan-out and whether it is a sanctioned automation account; check for preceding reads of ~/.ssh/id_* and authorized_keys on the source host. 2) Contain: isolate the source, revoke/rotate the implicated SSH keys, and disable key-based auth for the affected account fleet-wide. 3) Hunt: examine each destination host for the lambsys binary, cron persistence and C2 beacons; treat every successfully-reached host as compromised and pivot.
DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where RemotePort == 22 | summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(RemoteIP), Hosts=make_set(RemoteIP,100), Procs=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,10), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessParentFileName,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName | where DistinctHosts >= 10 | order by DistinctHosts desc
ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where DstPortNumber == 22 | summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(DstIpAddr), Hosts=make_set(DstIpAddr,100), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr | where DistinctHosts >= 10 | order by DistinctHosts desc
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) (@process.command_line:(*"StrictHostKeyChecking=no"* OR *"/.ssh/id_"* OR *authorized_keys*)) @process.name:(ssh OR sshpass OR scp)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=22 | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true), limit=max) | _count >= 10
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_hosts count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=22 by All_Traffic.src_ip | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_hosts >= 10 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_hosts count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=22 by All_Traffic.src_ip | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_hosts >= 10 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
lambsys XMRig miner: ipinfo.io geo-check and known cryptominer hashes/cmdline AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage where lambsys fetches a TAR-packed bespoke XMRig miner, queries ipinfo.io for geo-tuning/geo-fencing, and runs the miner. Article-specific: matches the named lambsys/XMRig hashes plus XMRig cmdline and the ipinfo.io discovery call. Rationale: Combines the article's named lambsys/XMRig hashes (incl. ddde47bf… miner and 46096a72… MD5) with XMRig-specific cmdline tokens and the ipinfo.io geo-fencing call — the hash and stratum/donate-level strings make this a low-FP impact detection.
ATT&CKT1496 T1614 T1016.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned XMRig benchmarking on a research/lab host
  • Legitimate apps calling ipinfo.io for geolocation
  • Crypto-mining performed knowingly on a dedicated rig
  • EDR/AV quarantine replays surfacing the hash post-cleanup
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "/opt/benchmark" and AccountName !in~ ("miner-lab")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process hash/command line against the IOCs and check host CPU for sustained 100% utilization plus stratum mining-pool egress. 2) Contain: kill the miner, isolate the host, and block the mining-pool destinations and ipinfo.io egress from server workloads. 3) Hunt: trace back to the lambsys dropper and Langflow RCE foothold, locate the TAR archive (created then wiped after launch), and sweep peer hosts for the same hashes and stratum traffic.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in ("ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2","71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc","33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df") or MD5 == "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--donate-level","stratum+tcp","ipinfo.io","xmrig") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5 | order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in ("ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2","71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc","33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df") or MD5 == "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--donate-level","stratum+tcp","ipinfo.io","xmrig") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5 | order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
