Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or SHA1 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or MD5 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or SHA1 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or MD5 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BleepingComputer
2026-06-30 5 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious 'Perplexity AI' Chromium extension flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to browser profile · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Browser egress to fake-Perplexity interception infra (perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Malicious 'Perplexity AI' Chromium extension flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to browser profile AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-disk install of the fake 'Search for perplexity ai' extension by its globally-unique Chrome Web Store ID landing in a Chromium browser's Extensions folder. Article-specific because the ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd is the single highest-fidelity IOC Microsoft published. Rationale: Pivots on the unique extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd (Microsoft IOC, cross-checked against the MS Security blog and The Hacker News); a Chromium browser writing this folder name to a profile is unambiguous and needs no thresholding. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/29/chromium-extension-uses-airelated-branding-redirect-browser-search/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4191060/malicious-chromium-extension-spoofs-perplexity-ai-to-hijack-browser-searches.html
ATT&CKT1176.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or IR analyst intentionally detonating/analyzing the extension sample on a sandbox host
  • DFIR tooling copying a captured browser profile (which contains the ID folder) onto an analyst workstation
  • Chrome profile sync restoring an old profile snapshot that still contains the extension before it was pulled from the store
  • EDR/AV quarantine relocating the extension folder, generating a file-write event under the ID
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device + user, and check the parent browser process and folder timestamp to see when the extension was sideloaded; confirm extension still present in chrome://extensions. 2) Contain: remove the extension by ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd from the user's browser, reset default search provider, and force-rotate the user's critical-account passwords per Microsoft guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 to confirm the host ever beaconed to perplexity-ai.online/oda.digital, and sweep all endpoints for the same ID folder to scope org-wide spread.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser egress to fake-Perplexity interception infra (perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) AICommand & Control High
Hunts a browser resolving/connecting to the typosquatted search-interception domain perplexity-ai.online, the operator domain oda.digital, or the onboarding page extension.tilda.ws used by the fake Perplexity extension. Article-specific because these exact domains carry the intercepted Omnibox queries and keystroke-level suggest_url traffic. Rationale: Uses the three exact domains Microsoft published (perplexity-ai.online = query/suggest_url interception endpoint, oda.digital = operator infra, extension.tilda.ws = onboarding); a browser touching perplexity-ai.online in particular is a clean true positive since the legitimate service is perplexity.ai. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/29/chromium-extension-uses-airelated-branding-redirect-browser-search/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately browsing an unrelated site hosted on Tilda's website builder under the shared extension.tilda.ws subdomain
  • oda.digital resolving for an unrelated benign service that happens to share the name
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation host deliberately visiting these domains during analysis
  • Security awareness/phishing-simulation platform replaying the IOC domains as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl has "perplexity-ai.online"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and the initiating browser; confirm whether the resolution targeted perplexity-ai.online (high confidence) vs oda.digital/extension.tilda.ws (verify context), and check timing against the extension install. 2) Contain: remove extension flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd, reset default search provider, and block the three domains at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 file-write to confirm install on the same host, enumerate every internal host resolving perplexity-ai.online to scope, and rotate passwords for accounts whose searches may have been logged.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-browser process writing Chromium 'Secure Preferences'/'Preferences' (Silent Swap sideload) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Silent Swap covert extension install: a non-browser process (the unsigned .NET BaseZipInstaller or Golang variant) writing to a Chromium 'Secure Preferences' or 'Preferences' file under a browser User Data profile. Normally only the browser itself writes these HMAC-protected files; a third-party writer indicates the malware tampering with protected settings to silently register the fake 'Google Notes' extension. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit covert-install mechanic: the malware modifies the browser's HMAC-protected 'Secure Preferences'/'Preferences' files (under User Data) from a non-browser installer. Limiting the writer to non-browser processes makes this very high-fidelity since legit modification is browser-exclusive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html • https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~andrei/cans20.pdf
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser profile migration/sync tools (e.g. third-party bookmark importers) writing Preferences
  • Enterprise browser management/GPO agents pushing managed extension policy
  • Antivirus or backup software touching the User Data folder and re-writing Preferences
  • Browser repair/reset utilities run by IT support
  • Roaming-profile redirection writing Preferences on logon
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and FolderPath; check if the writer is signed and known. Pull the modified 'Secure Preferences' and diff the 'extensions.settings' / 'extensions.ui.developer_mode' nodes for an unfamiliar extension ID claiming 'Google Notes'. 2) Contain: kill the installer process, isolate the host, and remove the rogue extension from every Chromium profile; reset Secure Preferences. Treat any crypto wallet addresses copied during the window as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writer's SHA256 across the fleet, check for self-deleted installers and ZIP retrievals, and look for the C2 connections in UC3.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where FolderPath has @"\User Data\"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\", @"\Vivaldi\", @"\Opera Software\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe","msedge_proxy.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\User Data\"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\", @"\Vivaldi\", @"\Opera Software\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7b3e9c2a-1d4f-4a8b-9c6e-2f5a8d1b4c30
status: experimental
description: Detects a non-browser process writing to a Chromium 'Secure Preferences' or 'Preferences' file, the covert extension-injection + HMAC-recalculation technique used by the Silent Swap crypto clipper to register a fake Google Notes extension.
references:

Single process force-terminating multiple Chromium browsers (Silent Swap profile-unlock precursor) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Silent Swap pre-injection step where the installer enumerates installed Chromium browsers and forcibly terminates each one to unlock the profile files before tampering. Flags a single non-browser initiator running taskkill against two or more distinct Chromium browser binaries within a short window. Rationale: Built on the article's stated behaviour that the installer 'forcibly terminates the browser process' for each detected Chromium profile before modifying its files. Requiring >=2 distinct browser targets from one initiator separates this from a normal single-browser restart. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT scripts that close all browsers before a software update or imaging
  • Browser updater/installer killing the running instance before applying an update
  • User-run cleanup batch files that taskkill multiple browsers
  • Endpoint management tools (SCCM/Intune) terminating browsers for forced updates
  • RMM agents closing browsers prior to maintenance
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("update.exe","setup.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","ccmexec.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the initiating process and parent of taskkill; legit cases trace to known updaters/RMM. Confirm whether a 'Secure Preferences' write (UC1) followed on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: if the killer is an unknown/unsigned binary, isolate the host and capture the binary before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiator hash, search for ZIP downloads and self-deletion (file delete of own image), and check UC3 C2 connections for that host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "taskkill.exe"
| extend BrowserKilled = tolower(extract(@"(?i)(chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera|opera_gx)\.exe", 1, ProcessCommandLine))
| where isnotempty(BrowserKilled)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize KilledBrowsers = make_set(BrowserKilled), KillCount = dcount(BrowserKilled), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 8) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where KillCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\taskkill.exe"
| extend BrowserKilled = tolower(extract(@"(?i)(chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera|opera_gx)\.exe", 1, CommandLine))
| where isnotempty(BrowserKilled)
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize KilledBrowsers = make_set(BrowserKilled), KillCount = dcount(BrowserKilled), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleCmds = make_set(CommandLine, 8) by Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where KillCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\taskkill.exe OR *\\TASKKILL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*chrome.exe* OR *msedge.exe* OR *brave.exe* OR *vivaldi.exe* OR *opera.exe*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\taskkill\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(?<Browser>chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera)\.exe", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=[count(field=Browser, distinct=true, as=DistinctBrowsers), collect([Browser])])
| DistinctBrowsers >= 2

Silent Swap / VPN Go clipper C2 and clipboard-exfil to known infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on host connections to the confirmed Silent Swap and 'VPN Go' clipboard-stealer infrastructure: the two exfiltration IPs (178.236.252.133, 77.91.123.187) and the Silent Swap C2/dead-drop domain set. The campaign uses EtherHiding (blockchain dead-drop resolver) to rotate live C2, so these named IOCs are the durable network pivot for backend wallet-substitution and clipboard exfil. Rationale: Uses the two exfil IPs stated in the article body (Socket's VPN Go finding) and the McAfee Silent Swap C2 domain set. EtherHiding rotates the live C2, so direct-IP plus the static domain list is the most durable network pivot; 'bucket-aws-s*' domains are attacker C2, not real AWS, so no CloudWatch query applies. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5142-etherhiding-distribute-malware
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001 T1657
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An exfil IP later reassigned to shared/CDN hosting serving benign traffic
  • Security tooling or sandbox detonating a sample and contacting the IOC IP
  • Threat-intel/research workstations intentionally resolving the C2 domains
  • A look-alike domain typo coincidentally matching a benign service
  • Proxy/egress appliance pre-fetching URLs for inspection
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","sense.exe","wireshark.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection and whether it is a browser (extension-driven exfil) or the installer. Confirm the host also shows UC1/UC2 activity. 2) Contain: block the IPs/domains at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and remove the rogue extension; rotate any secrets/seed phrases and warn the user that copied wallet addresses may have been swapped. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for the full domain list, pivot on the connecting process hash, and check for blockchain RPC traffic indicative of EtherHiding dead-drop resolution.

| append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("hell1-kitty.cc","alphazero1-endscape.cc","api-microservice-us1.com","fileless-storage-s3.cc","globalsnn1-new.cc","globalsnn2-new.cc","globalsnn3-new.cc","handle-me-sv1.com","hardware-office.cc","health-smooth-eu1.com","health-smooth-eu2.com","health-smooth-eu3.com","holiday-updateservice.com","memory-protection-layer1.cc","memory-protection-layer2.cc","my-smart-house1.com") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

GuardFall Exposes Open-Source AI Coding Agents to Decades-Old Shell Injection Risks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The safety check that is supposed to stop an AI coding agent from running a dangerous command can be walked straight past using a shell trick that has been public for decades. New research from&nbsp;Adversa AI, which is named the bypass GuardFall, found it works against ten of the eleven popular open-source coding and computer-use agents the firm tested. Only one, "Continue," was built to

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts AI-coding-agent-spawned shells running commands obfuscated to defeat plain-text blocklists: empty-quote/backslash-split binary names (r''m), base64 piped into sh/bash, or benign tools (find/dd) given destructive flags. This is the exact GuardFall evasion shape where bash rewrites the string after the agent's filter inspected it. Rationale: Uses the article's literal GuardFall evasion primitives (empty-quote split like r''m, base64-pipe-to-shell, destructive find/dd flags) anchored to the named open-source agent binaries as parents — the combination of agent-parent + shell-child + obfuscated cmdline is far higher-fidelity than any single clause. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1027.010 T1140 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running a build script that base64-decodes an embedded asset and pipes it to a shell installer
  • CI/dev tooling using find -delete to clean build artifacts
  • dd used for legitimate disk imaging by a sysadmin on a dev box
  • Shell aliases or generated scripts that happen to contain quote-adjacent tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","make ","cmake","docker build") and ProcessCommandLine has "-delete")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any base64; confirm the parent is an AI coding agent and whether the session was non-interactive/auto-exec. Identify the repo/working dir the agent was pointed at. 2) Contain: kill the agent + shell processes, revoke and rotate any credentials reachable from $HOME (~/.ssh, ~/.aws), and quarantine the host from prod networks. 3) Hunt: review the triggering repo/PR (especially fork PRs and in-repo config like .aider.conf.yml) for the injected instruction; sweep other dev hosts for the same agent-parent + obfuscated-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI Coding Agent Shell with Obfuscated Command (GuardFall)
id: 6f3c1d2a-9b4e-4f1a-8c77-2a1e5b9d0c44
description: Detects an AI coding agent spawning a shell whose command line uses GuardFall-style obfuscation (empty-quote split binaries, base64 piped to shell, destructive find/dd flags) to bypass plain-text command blocklists.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/guardfall-exposes-open-source-ai-coding.html
  - https://adversa.ai/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1027.010
  - attack.t1140
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/aider'
      - '/goose'
      - '/cline'
      - '/plandex'
      - '/opencode'
      - '/open-interpreter'
      - '/openhands'
      - '/swe-agent'
      - '/node'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
  selection_shell:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
  selection_obfusc:
    CommandLine|re: "(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\\s+-d.*\\|\\s*(ba)?sh|\\bdd\\s+.+of=/dev/|find\\s+.+-delete|find\\s+.+-exec\\s+rm"
  condition: selection_parent and selection_shell and selection_obfusc
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:(bash OR sh OR dash OR zsh)) (@process.command_line:(*"base64 -d"* OR *"-exec rm"* OR *-delete* OR *of=/dev/*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the GuardFall precondition: a named open-source coding agent invoked with an auto-execute / skip-permissions flag (--auto-exec, --auto-run, --auto-test, --yes-always, dangerously-skip-permissions) that then spawns a shell or interpreter non-interactively. This is the unattended configuration that lets an injected command actually run. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit auto-execute flag names (--auto-exec/--auto-run/--auto-test/dangerously-skip-permissions) AND the named agent binaries spawning a shell — the unattended-execution precondition the article says must be true for the attack to land, making it a high-fidelity governance/posture alert. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/01/claude_code_rule_cap_raises/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal CI pipeline that intentionally runs an agent unattended on trusted internal repos
  • Developer using --yes-always on their own local repo for a known refactor
  • Automated test harness invoking the agent with --auto-test against a sandboxed branch
  • Demo/eval scripts running an agent non-interactively in a throwaway container
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-runner","build-agent") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--auto-test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the agent run was sanctioned (internal trusted repo vs fork/external) and which repo/working dir it targeted; capture the child shell command lines. 2) Contain: if the repo source is untrusted or unknown, terminate the agent session and disable the auto-execute flag in the relevant wrapper/CI job; isolate the host pending review. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/CI runners running these agents with auto-exec flags, and correlate forward to credential-file reads or outbound connections from the spawned shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","interpreter")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--auto-exec","--auto-run","--auto-test","--yes-always","--no-confirm","dangerously-skip-permissions")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","interpreter")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("--auto-exec","--auto-run","--auto-test","--yes-always","--no-confirm","dangerously-skip-permissions")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GuardFall credential-theft payload: a shell or copy/transfer tool spawned by an AI coding agent that reads SSH keys, cloud credentials, or other home-folder secrets. Targets the article's stated impact — stealing 'SSH keys and cloud credentials to anything sitting in your home folder'. Rationale: Combines the article's named agent binaries as parent with the exact credential paths it calls out (SSH keys, AWS/cloud creds in $HOME) referenced by a read/copy/transfer child process — agent-spawned access to ~/.ssh or ~/.aws is well outside normal agent working-dir behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An agent legitimately tasked with configuring git over SSH or deploying via scp reading ~/.ssh/config
  • Developer-driven 'aws configure' or terraform run that the agent shells out to and which touches ~/.aws/credentials
  • Backup or dotfile-sync tooling invoked through the agent's shell
  • Agent reading ~/.docker/config.json to run an authorized image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws configure","git@","ssh -T","terraform") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the credential access matched the task the user gave the agent; capture the destination of any subsequent cp/scp/curl. 2) Contain: immediately rotate the specific keys/credentials touched (SSH keypairs, AWS access keys, kube tokens) and revoke sessions; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the same shell for outbound exfil shortly after the read, and review the source repo/PR that the agent was operating on.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout AIDelivery Low
Hunts the GuardFall initial-access vector where a malicious agent config file shipped inside a repository (the article calls out .aider.conf.yml) is written to disk by a VCS/clone or the agent itself, which can trigger the attack on the first accepted edit. Treats in-repo agent config as untrusted code. Rationale: Uses the exact config filename the article names as untrusted-code (.aider.conf.yml) written by a clone/checkout or the agent — a focused hunting pivot for the supply-chain delivery step, kept low-confidence/hunting because legitimate repos also ship this file. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/blog/the-approval-prompt-is-lying-to-you-symlink-rce-in-five-ai-coding-agents-claude-code-cursor-antigravity-copilot-grok-build/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately commits .aider.conf.yml to share project agent settings
  • Developer cloning their own trusted repo that contains the config
  • Templating/scaffolding tools generating an aider config
  • CI checkout of an internal repo that ships the file by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/internal-repos/","/trusted/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the contents of the written .aider.conf.yml for embedded auto-run/auto-commit settings, shell hooks, or instructions, and identify the source repo/PR (especially fork PRs). 2) Contain: if the repo is untrusted/external, prevent the agent from running against it, move $HOME to a throwaway folder per the article's guidance, and disable auto-execute. 3) Hunt: correlate forward to agent-spawned shells (UC1/UC2) and credential reads (UC3) on the same host within the session window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ (".aider.conf.yml",".aider.conf.yaml","aider.conf.yml")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","node","python","python3","aider","tar","unzip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ (".aider.conf.yml",".aider.conf.yaml","aider.conf.yml")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git","node","python","python3","aider","tar","unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"

    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

What the Numbers Say About FIFA 2026 Cyber Risk

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The FIFA World Cup 2026 opened on June 11. By that date, according to Check Point Research, the fraud infrastructure targeting it had already been built, staged, and partially deployed. Threat actor activity was pre-planned, months out, across three sectors and at least ten languages. Check Point Exposure Management published the FIFA World Cup 2026 Cyber Threat Report this month, covering
