Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains · [LLM] Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the specific FIFA 2026 brand-impersonation domains staged by the Check Point / Group-IB-tracked fraud infrastructure (hospitality, store, and gambling lures). Article-specific because it pins the named registered domains rather than a generic 'newly-registered domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the seven concrete lookalike domains from the article's IOC bundle (www-fifa.me/.co, 26-fifa.com, op.shop-26fifa.com, fifaofficialstore.shop, fifa2026guess.com, fortune-worldcup2026.com.cn); these are dedicated fraud-only domains so any resolution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the FBI IC3 PSA and Check Point's research blog which independently confirm the campaign and several of the same domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/ • https://www.gblock.app/articles/fifa-2026-phishing-wave-fake-domains-email-scams
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel platform manually browsing the domain during triage
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox / SOAR enrichment visiting the domain from a known scanning host
  • Secure web gateway pre-fetch or link-rewrite service resolving the URL on the user's behalf
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor crawling the domain from corporate ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-sandbox","svc-urlscan") and DeviceName !in~ ("SOC-SANDBOX01","PROXY-SCAN01")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the host/user and the initiating process from DeviceNetworkEvents — confirm it was a browser/mail client (real user) vs a sandbox/proxy host, and whether a file download or credential-entry POST followed within 5 min. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole/block the domain at DNS and the secure web gateway tenant-wide; if the user submitted data, force a password reset + revoke sessions and isolate the host if a payload landed. 3) HUNT: pivot on the resolved IP and registrar pattern (.top, GoDaddy/Hostinger/Namecheap/Porkbun/IONOS) to surface sibling FIFA lookalikes the same host or org touched; review EmailEvents for the delivering message.
let fifaDomains = dynamic(["www-fifa.me","www-fifa.co","26-fifa.com","shop-26fifa.com","op.shop-26fifa.com","fifaofficialstore.shop","fifa2026guess.com","fortune-worldcup2026.com.cn"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (fifaDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email whose sender domain (envelope or header-from) or embedded URL belongs to the FIFA World Cup 2026 fraud domains — the article notes a subset have MX records configured for reply-path impersonation and password-reset interception. Article-specific via the named domains rather than a generic spoofing rule. Rationale: Anchors on the same seven named fraud domains but on the mail vector (SenderFromDomain / SenderMailFromDomain / embedded URL), targeting the reply-path-impersonation and password-reset-interception use the article calls out for the MX-enabled subset. Domains corroborated by FBI IC3 and Check Point; mail tracing is uniquely a Defender-for-O365 signal, so other platforms are left blank. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation platform using a FIFA-themed lure domain that overlaps a string
  • Brand-protection vendor sending sample/takedown-notice mail referencing the domains
  • Threat-intel newsletter or this very article being forwarded internally with the domains in the body (URL match on a benign report)
  • Quarantined/blocked messages surfacing in the hunt even though they never reached a user (DeliveryAction = Blocked/Quarantine)
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","JunkFolder") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishsimvendor.com"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation — prioritize messages Delivered to Inbox; check whether the recipient clicked (UrlClickEvents) or replied. 2) CONTAIN: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain and embedded URL, and if any recipient entered credentials or replied to a reply-path lure, force password reset + revoke tokens. 3) HUNT: search for the same sender infrastructure (shared IP/SPF record) hitting other mailboxes and correlate recipients against the UC1 network/DNS hits to find users who both received and visited the domain.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 forged OIDC Technician self-registration AIExploitation High
Hunts the server-side footprint of the SimpleHelp OIDC authentication bypass (CVE-2026-48558): an unauthenticated attacker forges an OIDC token and the SimpleHelp server logs a brand-new 'Technician' account registration. Surfaces the registered technician identity so analysts can compare it against the known technician roster. Rationale: Uses the exact SimpleHelp server.log strings Horizon3.ai published for CVE-2026-48558 ('Registering technician login for', 'Configuration save requested') — these are emitted on the OIDC token-forgery account creation and are the earliest detectable exploit artifact. SPL is a raw log search (no CIM datamodel covers SimpleHelp app logs). Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1190 T1606
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new technician/contractor via OIDC SSO
  • Admin testing or migrating the OIDC/Azure AD IdP configuration
  • MSP adding a new analyst account during shift handover
  • SimpleHelp version upgrade re-registering existing technicians
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the RegisteredTechnician value and compare against the approved technician roster; check the IdP for a matching real user and the source IP of the registration. 2) Contain: if the technician is unrecognised, disable/delete the account in SimpleHelp, revoke its sessions, and block the source IP; confirm the server is patched to the fixed SimpleHelp build. 3) Hunt: review server.log for scripts/files pushed by that technician and pivot to managed endpoints for node.exe/jquery.js execution (TaskWeaver).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "Registering technician login for" or SyslogMessage has "Configuration save requested"
| extend RegisteredTechnician = extract(@"Registering technician login for\s+([^\s""']+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, RegisteredTechnician, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog ("Registering technician login for" OR "Configuration save requested")
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype="simplehelp:server" "Registering technician login for"
| rex "Registering technician login for\s+(?<registered_technician>[^\s\"']+)"
| table _time host registered_technician _raw
| sort - _time
SimpleHelp Remote Access process spawning Node.js / script interpreters AIExploitation High
Detects the SimpleHelp endpoint agent ('Remote Access.exe' / 'remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe') spawning script interpreters or LOLBins on a managed host — the post-exploitation execution channel a forged Technician uses to drop TaskWeaver. Article-specific because TaskWeaver runs via node.exe pushed through the trusted RMM channel. Rationale: SimpleHelp's confirmed endpoint binary names ('Remote Access.exe', 'remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe') as parent of interpreters captures the trusted-RMM command-execution channel the article describes ('transferring files and executing commands on systems managed through the server'). node.exe is included because TaskWeaver runs via node.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-163a • https://forums.malwarebytes.com/topic/303064-simplehelp-remoteaccesswinlauncherexe-false-positive/
ATT&CKT1219 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Technician running cmd/powershell interactively for legitimate remote support
  • RMM-pushed patching/automation scripts (powershell/cmd) during maintenance windows
  • A legitimately RMM-deployed Node.js application or installer
  • certutil/curl used by IT for legitimate file transfer during a support session
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("jquery.js","-enc","-EncodedCommand","FromBase64String","\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\Public\\") or FileName =~ "node.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — benign support uses readable commands; flag obfuscated/base64 cmdlines or node.exe loading a .js from temp/AppData. Confirm the initiating technician is approved (cross-ref UC1). 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host, kill the process tree, and suspend the SimpleHelp technician account driving the session. 3) Hunt: search the same device for node.exe executing jquery.js, outbound dev-tunnels.com, and connections to 96.126.130.126:58942.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe","RemoteAccess.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe","RemoteAccess.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TaskWeaver loader: node.exe executing jquery.js AIInstallation High
Hunts the TaskWeaver Node.js loader, which the article states is 'delivered as jquery.js and executed through node.exe'. A Node runtime executing a script masquerading as the browser jQuery library is a high-fidelity, attack-specific signal. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's loader description: TaskWeaver 'delivered as jquery.js and executed through node.exe'. jQuery is a browser-side library, so a node.exe command line referencing jquery.js is anomalous and campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer with an unusual build/test script literally named jquery.js run under Node (rare)
  • An npm package whose test harness references a file named jquery.js
  • Server-side rendering frameworks bundling a file path containing 'jquery.js'
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\","\\Public\\","\\ProgramData\\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture FolderPath/SHA256 of node.exe and the jquery.js location; legitimate hits resolve under a project/node_modules tree, malicious ones run from temp/AppData/Public or via the RMM session. 2) Contain: isolate the host, collect the jquery.js file, kill node.exe, and submit the hash for blocking. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same node.exe PID/host for outbound dev-tunnels.com beacons and exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942, and check the parent for SimpleHelp Remote Access.exe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TaskWeaver C2 beacon to dev-tunnels.com from node.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the TaskWeaver C2 channel: node.exe resolving/connecting to a.dev-tunnels.com (Microsoft Dev Tunnels abused for C2). Scoped to a node.exe initiator to separate malicious tunneling from legitimate developer Dev Tunnels usage. Rationale: Uses the article's named C2 host (a.dev-tunnels.com) constrained to a node.exe initiator (TaskWeaver runtime). Dev Tunnels is a legitimate Microsoft service, so process scoping is required; Sentinel DnsEvents cannot attribute process, so confidence is Medium there. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers using Microsoft Dev Tunnels for legitimate port forwarding from VS/VS Code (which uses Node-based tooling)
  • CI/CD agents creating dev tunnels for remote debugging
  • Node-based local web apps exposed via Dev Tunnels for testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the node.exe is a known dev workflow vs. the jquery.js loader (cross-ref UC3) and review the InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed-dev, isolate host, block the dev-tunnels subdomain at the proxy, and kill node.exe. 3) Hunt: check the host for jquery.js execution, SimpleHelp Remote Access.exe parentage, and follow-on exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "dev-tunnels.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Name has "dev-tunnels.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, IPAddresses, QueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Djinn Stealer multi-store credential harvesting by node.exe AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Djinn Stealer second stage: the TaskWeaver node.exe runtime touching files across multiple distinct credential classes (cloud CLI, SSH/GPG keys, infra tooling, AI-assistant configs, crypto wallets) in a short window. The cross-class fan-out (>=3 categories) is the behavioural signature the article enumerates. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit target list for Djinn Stealer (AWS/Azure/GCP/OCI configs, SSH keys, Docker/Helm/Vault, npm/pnpm, AI-assistant configs for Claude/Gemini/Codex, crypto wallets). Requiring node.exe to touch >=3 distinct credential classes turns a noisy file-access query into a stealer-fan-out signal. No Sigma (threshold/correlation); Datadog omitted as auditd schema here lacks a reliable file-path facet for credential reads. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based dev tooling legitimately reading cloud creds (serverless framework, aws-cdk, pulumi, wrangler) on a developer workstation
  • Dotfile-sync or backup agents enumerating home-directory config
  • An IaC pipeline node process reading .terraform/.kube/.docker during a deploy
  • IDE extensions (VS Code, run via Node) indexing project credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","remoteaccesswinlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review SampleFiles/Categories — a genuine dev tool stays within one ecosystem (e.g. only .aws), while Djinn spans cloud+keys+ai+wallet; confirm node.exe lineage (jquery.js / SimpleHelp parent). 2) Contain: isolate the host and treat every touched credential as compromised — rotate cloud keys, SSH/GPG keys, npm/registry tokens, AI-assistant API keys, and sweep wallets. 3) Hunt: look for a TAR/GZIP staging file written by node.exe and outbound transfer to 96.126.130.126:58942; expand credential rotation to any production systems reachable with the stolen keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws", @"\.azure", @"\.config\gcloud", @"\.oci", @"\.ssh", @"\.docker", @"\.kube", @"\.config\gh", @"\.gnupg", @"\.npmrc", @"\.config\helm", @"\.vault-token", @"\.claude", @"\.config\anthropic", @"\.gemini", @"\.codeium", @"\.electrum", @"\Login Data", @"wallet.dat")
| extend CredCategory = case(
    FolderPath has @"\.aws" or FolderPath has @"\.azure" or FolderPath has @"\.config\gcloud" or FolderPath has @"\.oci", "cloud",
    FolderPath has @"\.ssh" or FolderPath has @"\.gnupg", "keys",
    FolderPath has @"\.docker" or FolderPath has @"\.kube" or FolderPath has @"\.config\helm" or FolderPath has @"\.vault-token", "infra",
    FolderPath has @"\.claude" or FolderPath has @"\.config\anthropic" or FolderPath has @"\.gemini" or FolderPath has @"\.codeium", "ai",
    FolderPath has @"\.electrum" or FolderPath has @"wallet.dat", "wallet",
    FolderPath has @"\Login Data", "browser",
    "other")
| summarize DistinctCategories = dcount(CredCategory), Categories = make_set(CredCategory), FilesTouched = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 20), StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctCategories >= 3
| order by EndTime desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.aws", @"\.azure", @"\.config\gcloud", @"\.oci", @"\.ssh", @"\.docker", @"\.kube", @"\.config\gh", @"\.gnupg", @"\.npmrc", @"\.vault-token", @"\.claude", @"\.config\anthropic", @"\.gemini", @"\.electrum", @"\Login Data", @"wallet.dat")

| regex("\\\\(\\.aws|\\.azure|\\.ssh|\\.docker|\\.kube|\\.gnupg|gcloud|\\.oci|\\.claude|\\.gemini|\\.electrum|\\.vault-token)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctFiles))
| DistinctFiles >= 4

| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_path) as files_touched values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="node.exe" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*.aws*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.ssh*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.docker*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.azure*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*gcloud*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.kube*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.gnupg*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.claude*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.electrum*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name

Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the encrypted-archive exfiltration step: an outbound connection to the attacker IP 96.126.130.126 on TCP port 58942, where Djinn Stealer ships the AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048-encrypted TAR.GZ of harvested credentials. The exact IP+non-standard-port pair is the article's hardest IOC. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exfil endpoint (96.126.130.126:58942). The IP+uncommon-port pair is highly specific; the Defender/Falcon variants also surface the initiating process so analysts can confirm it is the node.exe/Djinn runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1571 T1560.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Highly unlikely for this exact IP+port; possible only if a benign internal service is later assigned 96.126.130.126 (a Linode-range IP)
  • An internet-wide scanner or threat-intel sensor in your org deliberately probing the IOC
  • Penetration-test/purple-team replaying the IOC during an authorized exercise
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and InitiatingProcessFileName; any hit is treated as confirmed exfil given the IOC specificity — estimate bytes_out/NetworkBytes to gauge data volume. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 96.126.130.126 (and the /24) at the egress firewall, and kill the responsible process. 3) Hunt: assume credentials enumerated by Djinn (UC5) are exfiltrated — force org-wide rotation of cloud/SSH/registry/AI keys, hunt other hosts beaconing to the same IP, and review SimpleHelp for additional compromised endpoints.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP == "96.126.130.126" and RemotePort == 58942
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr == "96.126.130.126" and DstPortNumber == 58942
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

An in-depth analysis of Umbrij, a new tool used by the ToddyCat APT group to compromise corporate email communications in Gmail. The attack targeted OAuth authorization tokens, allowing threat actors to gain access to Google services.

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1134.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1528 T1574.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) · [LLM] Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/launch step where ToddyCat created a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp to run a digitally-signed sideload host. Kaspersky never creates a task with this name, so any occurrence of the string is malicious by definition. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masquerading task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' called out in the article's Execution section; it is a fixed, unique string no legitimate product emits. Cross-checked Securelist part 2 and the ToddyCat series. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually re-creating the task name during IR reproduction/testing
  • An internal red-team emulating ToddyCat TTPs
  • A detection-content lab importing the IOC string into a test task
  • Documentation/scripts that reference the task name in comments being scanned by inventory tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scheduled task definition (Actions/Exec path) and the signed binary it launches; verify the signer and whether the path is a writable dir (Users\Public, Temp, vss). 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the launched binary + any same-folder DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary hash and folder across the fleet; check for the BDS.exe/log.dll sideload chain and Chromium remote-debugging launches on the same host within +/- 1h.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RegistryKey has @"\TaskCache\" and RegistryKey has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=RegistryKey, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4702, 4699)
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Activity, EventID, EventData

ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact sideload pairs ToddyCat abused to launch Umbrij: BDSubWiz.exe/bds.exe loading log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe loading Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll, and GoogleDesktop.exe loading GoogleServices.dll, when the module loads from a user-writable directory or matches the known log.dll hashes. Rationale: Uses the exact legitimate-host -> malicious-DLL pairs named in the article (BDSubWiz/bds.exe+log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder+VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop+GoogleServices.dll), plus the writable paths and log.dll/BDS.exe MD5s read directly from in-article screenshot image1.jpeg (4C39087.../22AAEB49... and 28CB7B26...). Writable-path constraint removes legitimate in-product loads. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by writable-path filter)
  • Visual Studio test runs loading VideoRecorderEngine.dll from the VS install directory
  • A legacy Google Desktop install in Program Files loading GoogleServices.dll
  • Security testing/EDR validation copying these binaries into a sandbox temp folder
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded DLL hash against the known IOCs and verify the host binary is running from Users\Public/Temp/vss rather than its vendor install path; check the DLL export (LogInit) and ConfuserEx markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and host binary, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: from the host process, pivot to child Chromium launches with --remote-debugging-port and outbound connections to *.googleapis.com; sweep fleet for the same DLL hashes and the KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe") and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
     or MD5 in~ ("4C39087E5229A70F0215AFB8B7083091","22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Dll=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Umbrij tool by its distinctive command-line parameters documented in the article, including the example invocation of a renamed BDSubWiz.exe with -regex and -deepsearch. These switch names are unique to Umbrij. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim Umbrij CLI parameters enumerated in the article's parameter table (-deepsearch, -runas-currentuser, -domainAd, -savepdf, -debugport, -browser). These switch spellings are tool-specific and not used by mainstream software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation tool that happens to use a -debugport plus -browser flag combination
  • Red-team replaying Umbrij invocations during an authorized engagement
  • An unrelated CLI utility using the generic -savepdf flag (mitigated by requiring the ToddyCat-specific switch set)
  • Developer testing of a custom .NET tool with similar argument naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the executing binary; resolve which browser/path/port were targeted (-path, -browser, -debugport) and whether -runas-currentuser/-user indicates token impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and revoke/rotate the affected user's Google OAuth sessions and tokens immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with the parent sideload host (BDS.exe/log.dll), Chromium --remote-debugging-port launches, and outbound *.googleapis.com traffic on the same host and account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge/Chromium with a remote debugging port (often headless) to drive the user's live Gmail session. Flags browser processes carrying --remote-debugging-port when spawned by the sideload hosts or run headless. Rationale: Built on the article's explicit description of launching a Chromium browser in headless mode and connecting via the remote debugging port; pairs the --remote-debugging-port flag with the article-specific sideload parents or the --headless evasion flag to suppress legitimate interactive debugging. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1185 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation with --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • CI build agents driving headless Chrome for screenshot or PDF generation
  • VS Code / IDE debugging a web app via the Chrome DevTools Protocol
  • Synthetic monitoring agents launching headless browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","devenv.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and folder — a CI/automation tool from a dev path is likely benign; a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/bds/GoogleDesktop or from Users\Public/Temp is malicious. Note the --remote-debugging-port value and target profile. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the browser and parent, and immediately revoke the user's Google sessions/refresh tokens and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com connections from the same host/account and to the Umbrij CLI-switch and log.dll sideload detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\chromium.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access/exfil step where Umbrij (running as a renamed signed binary, not a browser) exchanges the stolen OAuth authorization code for an access token and pulls Gmail via the Google API. Flags the sideload hosts contacting *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com. Rationale: Combines the article's OAuth-code-to-access-token exchange and Google-API access with the sideload host names confirmed in screenshot image1.jpeg; a renamed Bitdefender/VSTest/GoogleDesktop binary speaking directly to Google OAuth/Gmail APIs (work normally done only by the browser) is a strong, low-FP anomaly. Sentinel left empty because process-attributed network telemetry to these hosts is not available in standard Sentinel tables (would require Sysmon EID3 ingestion). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1528 T1114.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Google Desktop legacy install (in Program Files) performing update/sync checks to googleapis.com
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent telemetry/update traffic to a Google-hosted CDN (rare; mitigated by host-name + writable-path context)
  • Security testing of the binaries in a lab with live internet
  • A renamed-but-benign internal tool reusing one of these file names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signer and verify it is the renamed sideload host rather than the genuine vendor product; pull the destination URLs and timing relative to any browser remote-debug launch. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the binary, and revoke the affected Google account's OAuth tokens/refresh tokens and active sessions; review Google Workspace audit logs for token grants and bulk message reads. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where these binaries reach Google APIs, correlate with the log.dll sideload and KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, and check for mailbox data staged/exfiltrated.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2 Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("bdsubwiz.exe", "log.dll", "vstestvideorecorder.exe", "qualitytools.videorecorderengine.dll", "googledesktop.exe", "googleservices.dll", "bds.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\Users\Public\BDSubWiz.exe", "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User", "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge\User", "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\BackupFiles\", "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge\BackupFiles\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
