Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Blackfield (BlackFL) ransomware encryption: .BlackFL extension + BlackField_ReadMe.txt note drop · [LLM] Blackfield ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via WMIC (inhibit recovery) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Blackfield (BlackFL) ransomware encryption: .BlackFL extension + BlackField_ReadMe.txt note drop AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the file-system signature of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware encryption: files renamed/created with the unique '.BlackFL' extension and the dropping of the 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt' (or Feb-2026 variant 'BlackField-ReadMe.txt') ransom note. Both strings are unique to this family — corroborated across PCrisk, EnigmaSoft and WatchGuard — so this is article/campaign-specific rather than a generic mass-rename heuristic. Rationale: Anchored on two strings unique to this family and confirmed by second sources (PCrisk, WatchGuard): the '.BlackFL' encrypted-file extension and the 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt'/'BlackField-ReadMe.txt' ransom note. Neither appears in benign software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware • https://www.watchguard.com/wgrd-security-hub/ransomware-tracker/blackfield • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or researcher host holding sample files that already carry the '.BlackFL' extension
  • A security awareness/IR test or purple-team exercise intentionally dropping a file named BlackField_ReadMe.txt
  • Backup or quarantine archive that preserved previously-encrypted '.BlackFL' files being restored to a host
  • A threat-intel document or zip containing the ransom note text saved with the literal note filename
Suppression filter
| where AffectedFolders >= 2 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1   // single isolated .BlackFL sample with no note is likely a researcher/backup artifact
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the alerting DeviceName, pull the InitiatingProcess/SHA256 that wrote the files and check whether '.BlackFL' files span multiple folders (mass-rename = live encryption vs. a single benign sample). Confirm the BlackField_ReadMe.txt note timestamp. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately network-isolate the host via EDR, suspend/kill the initiating process, and disable the involved account; preserve a memory image before reimaging. 3) HUNT: Pivot the initiating-process SHA256 and the writing account across all hosts; search for the WMIC shadow-copy deletion (UC2), recent SMB share enumeration, and lateral logons from the same account to scope blast radius across the Nidec Chaun Choung subnet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".BlackFL"
    or FileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"
| summarize EncryptedFileCount = countif(FileName endswith ".BlackFL"),
            RansomNoteDropped = countif(FileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"),
            AffectedFolders = dcount(FolderPath),
            SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            InitiatingProcess = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            InitiatingProcessSHA256 = any(InitiatingProcessSHA256),
            InitiatingCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
        by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId
| where EncryptedFileCount >= 1 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".BlackFL"
    or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"
| summarize EncryptedFileCount = countif(TargetFileName endswith ".BlackFL"),
            RansomNoteDropped = countif(TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"),
            AffectedPaths = dcount(TargetFilePath),
            SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Process = any(ActingProcessName)
        by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId
| where EncryptedFileCount >= 1 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Blackfield (BlackFL) Ransomware Encryption Artifacts
id: 7c2f1e84-3b6a-4d2e-9f10-2a1b9c8d4e51
description: Detects file-system artifacts of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware - files renamed/created with the .BlackFL extension or the BlackField_ReadMe.txt ransom note being dropped.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
  - https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1486
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.BlackFL'
  selection_note:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt'
      - 'BlackField-ReadMe.txt'
  condition: selection_ext or selection_note
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.BlackFL OR *.blackfl OR *.BLACKFL) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\BlackField_ReadMe.txt OR *\\BlackField-ReadMe.txt OR *\\blackfield_readme.txt))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\.BlackFL$|BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| count >= 1
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_path) as folder_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.BlackFL" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField_ReadMe.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField-ReadMe.txt") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_path) as folder_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.BlackFL" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField_ReadMe.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField-ReadMe.txt") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Blackfield ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via WMIC (inhibit recovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the pre-encryption recovery-inhibition step documented for Blackfield/BlackFL: use of WMIC.exe to delete Volume Shadow Copies (with vssadmin as a fallback variant). Pairs with the encryption UC to give execution + impact coverage of the same intrusion before files are locked. Rationale: BlackField is documented (PCrisk/SOCRadar) to terminate recovery options by using WMIC.exe to delete Volume Shadow Copies; the wmic shadowcopy-delete and vssadmin delete-shadows command shapes are the concrete invocations. Medium fidelity because legitimate backup tooling can issue similar commands, hence the FP filter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware • https://www.ransomware.live/group/Blackfield • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
ATT&CKT1490 T1047
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam / Acronis / Commvault backup jobs running pre-snapshot shadow-copy cleanup
  • Sysadmin manually troubleshooting VSS (vssadmin list/delete shadows) during storage maintenance
  • Windows imaging or DISM operations recycling shadow storage
  • SQL Server / Exchange backup maintenance scripts invoking WMIC shadowcopy operations
  • Endpoint management/SCCM task that prunes shadow copies on a schedule
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","veeam.backup.manager.exe","acronis.exe","clussvc.exe","vsnapvss.exe","ccmexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the parent process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a backup product (veeam, acronis) or services.exe-spawned admin tool is likely benign; an unsigned/unusual parent or one running from a temp path is high-risk. Check the same host for '.BlackFL' files (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: If the parent is not an approved backup agent, isolate the host immediately and disable the executing account before encryption completes. 3) HUNT: Sweep all hosts for the same parent SHA256, recent backup-deletion or bcdedit recovery-tampering commands, and the BlackField ransom note; review the account's logon history for lateral movement into the affected subsidiary network.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "shadowcopy" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete")
    or (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Blackfield Ransomware Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via WMIC
id: 2d9a7f3c-1e4b-4a8d-bc60-5f3e2d1a9b74
description: Detects WMIC.exe (with vssadmin fallback) deleting Volume Shadow Copies, the documented recovery-inhibition step of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware prior to encryption.
references:
  - https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1490
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1047
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wmic:
    Image|endswith: '\wmic.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'shadowcopy'
      - 'delete'
  selection_vss:
    Image|endswith: '\vssadmin.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'delete'
      - 'shadows'
  condition: selection_wmic or selection_vss
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\wmic.exe OR *\\WMIC.exe OR *\\WMIC.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)) OR (@Image:(*\\vssadmin.exe OR *\\VSSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*delete* AND *shadows*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wmic|vssadmin)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/shadow/i
| CommandLine=/delete/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT

AirDrop and Quick Share Flaws Let Nearby Attackers Trigger Crashes and Bypass Checks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two researchers have found six security flaws in AirDrop and Quick Share, the wireless features that beam files between nearby devices with no cables or shared network. An attacker within wireless range, with just a laptop and no prior connection, can crash the sharing service on a Mac or iPhone set to receive from anyone, with no tap or prompt. The same research found Quick Share flaws that

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the Google Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) crashing and restarting repeatedly on a single host, consistent with a nearby/same-LAN attacker repeatedly colliding two connections to trigger the use-after-free described in the CISPA research. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times in 10 minutes is not normal lifecycle behaviour. Rationale: Uses the concrete Windows Quick Share client binary name (nearby_share.exe, publisher Google LLC) confirmed via the SpyShelter process DB, plus the article's claim of a crash triggered when two connections collide. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times / crashing repeatedly is the observable footprint of the local UAF DoS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app instability after a Windows feature update or a corrupt Quick Share install causing repeated WER crashes
  • User repeatedly relaunching Quick Share manually from the system tray after it hangs on a large legitimate transfer
  • Quick Share auto-update mid-session restarting the client process several times
  • Driver/Wi-Fi adapter resets on the host destabilising the Bluetooth+Wi-Fi stack Quick Share depends on
  • Sysmon/Defender double-reporting the same process start during high event volume
Suppression filter
// Suppress benign updater-driven restarts
| where SampleFolder !has "\\Update\\" and SampleCompany has_any ("Google", "")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host actually has Quick Share for Windows installed and pull the bin(10m) of nearby_share.exe starts / Application Error 1000 events; check whether the device was in a crowded shared space (airport/conference/office Wi-Fi) at crash time and whether CFG is enforced on the binary. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user close Quick Share and set visibility off 'Everyone' (out of receive mode); if the crash loop persists, isolate the host's Wi-Fi/Bluetooth or network-isolate and ensure the Google-patched Quick Share build is installed. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'nearby_share.exe spawning a shell/LOLBin' on the same host/time window to rule out the crash being escalated to code execution, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the inbound peer IP that preceded the crashes.
// Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) crash-restart loop — sustained proximity/LAN UAF DoS
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize LaunchCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleFolder = any(FolderPath), SampleCompany = any(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
        by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where LaunchCount >= 5   // >=5 (re)starts of the Quick Share tray app in 10 min = crash loop; normal lifecycle is 1 start per logon
| order by LastSeen desc
// Application Error (Event ID 1000) faulting on nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows)
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source == "Application Error" and EventID == 1000
| where RenderedDescription has "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleDescription = any(RenderedDescription)
        by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CrashCount >= 3   // >=3 app-error crashes of Quick Share in 10 min
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\nearby_share.exe OR *\\Nearby_Share.exe OR *\\NEARBY_SHARE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\nearby_share\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
| count >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="nearby_share.exe" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="nearby_share.exe" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution AIExploitation High
Hunts for the Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) spawning a command shell, scripting host, or download-capable LOLBin as a child. The CISPA research notes the Windows use-after-free is plausibly exploitable for code execution because Control Flow Guard is disabled in the app; nearby_share.exe legitimately spawns no such children, so any is high-fidelity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's specific claim that the Windows Quick Share UAF is plausibly exploitable for code execution (CFG off). Uses the concrete parent binary nearby_share.exe; this tray app has no legitimate reason to spawn cmd/powershell/mshta/rundll32 etc., making the parent->child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quick Share updater logic shelling out to a maintenance/cleanup script during an in-place upgrade
  • Enterprise software-management agent injecting a child process under nearby_share.exe for inventory
  • Security tooling (EDR/DLP) reparenting or hollowing nearby_share.exe causing an apparent child spawn
  • An IT helpdesk troubleshooting script launched while Quick Share happened to be the foreground process (rare reparent)
Suppression filter
// Drop known updater path if it legitimately invokes cmd in your environment
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Quick Share\\Update\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — decode any encoded/obfuscated args, check the child's network connections and file writes, and confirm whether a Quick Share crash (UC1) or an inbound peer connection immediately preceded this on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and capture nearby_share.exe memory; block the child binary hash if attacker-supplied. 3) HUNT: Sweep the fleet for the same parent->child pair, pivot on the child's C2 destinations across DeviceNetworkEvents, and verify all endpoints run Google's patched Quick Share build.
// nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows) spawning a shell/LOLBin child — possible UAF -> code execution
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// 4688: nearby_share.exe spawning shell/LOLBin
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\nearby_share.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

CVE-2026-33825 (BlueHammer) exposure: unpatched Microsoft Defender engine AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints still vulnerable to the BlueHammer Defender LPE (CVE-2026-33825), a CISA-KEV ransomware-flagged flaw with a passed FCEB patch deadline. Exposure-management pivot to prioritise the Defender Antimalware Platform 4.18.26050.3011 update before the local-privesc primitive can be abused. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CVE (CVE-2026-33825) and the corroborated patched platform build 4.18.26050.3011; Defender TVM maps the CVE directly, so this is a high-fidelity exposure list. Pre-extracted MD5s were uncorroborated in any second source and excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/bluehammer-redsun-windows-defender-cve-2026-33825-zero-day-vulnerability-explained • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-33825 • https://github.com/fleetdm/fleet/issues/45633
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices already on Defender platform 4.18.26050.3011+ but with a stale TVM snapshot pending re-scan
  • Decommissioned or long-offline endpoints still present in inventory
  • Air-gapped hosts where Defender auto-update is deliberately disabled under compensating controls
  • Non-Windows assets mis-tagged in the vuln-scanner feed
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the device list and cross-check each against current Defender platform version (4.18.26050.3011+ is patched); drop hosts already updated. 2) Contain: force the Defender Antimalware Platform update on remaining hosts; for internet-facing or high-value systems apply attack-surface-reduction and restrict local logon until patched. 3) Hunt: for any host that stayed unpatched past the April patch window, pivot to UC2/UC3 (MsMpEng writes to System32 / MsMpEng child process) over the exposure window to confirm the primitive wasn't already abused.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-33825"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-33825"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-33825" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - count
Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe) writes executable into System32 — BlueHammer LPE payoff AIExploitation Medium
Detects the CVE-2026-33825 TOCTOU/junction primitive succeeding: the SYSTEM-privileged Defender engine MsMpEng.exe is coerced (via oplock + NTFS junction redirect) into creating an executable/DLL/script inside a protected OS directory. MsMpEng creating new executable content in System32/SysWOW64 is highly abnormal and is the article's privilege-escalation write-as-SYSTEM step. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated BlueHammer mechanism (oplock + NTFS junction redirecting MsMpEng.exe's SYSTEM-context write into C:\Windows\System32). The pivot — Defender's own engine creating new executable content in a protected OS directory — is near-zero baseline and directly evidences the LPE primitive firing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/bluehammer-redsun-windows-defender-cve-2026-33825-zero-day-vulnerability-explained • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/windows-zero-day-bluehammer • https://denizhalil.com/2026/06/12/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-vulnerability-analysis/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender remediating genuine malware that resides in System32 (typically FileDeleted/FileRenamed, not FileCreated — excluded by ActionType scope)
  • Defender restoring a falsely-quarantined legitimate System32 binary from the quarantine store (excluded by PreviousFolderPath filter)
  • Defender platform self-update writing into its own Platform directory (excluded by path scope)
  • EICAR/AV-test artefacts being cleaned during validation testing
Suppression filter
| where not(PreviousFolderPath has_any (@"\Quarantine\", @"\Windows Defender\")) and not(FolderPath has @"\Windows Defender\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the file MsMpEng wrote (FileName/SHA256/FolderPath); submit hash to TI, and check whether the same host shows a recent NTFS junction/reparse-point creation or oplock activity in a user-writable temp dir just prior. 2) Contain: isolate the host — a SYSTEM-level write succeeded; quarantine the planted file, and snapshot for forensics before the binary is loaded/executed. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (MsMpEng spawning a child) and to subsequent execution of the dropped path as SYSTEM; review local SAM/account changes and new local admins, and confirm Defender platform is on 4.18.26050.3011+.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\")
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".sys" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".scr"
| where not(PreviousFolderPath has_any (@"\Quarantine\", @"\Windows Defender\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has "MsMpEng.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe", "dll", "sys", "bat", "ps1", "cmd", "scr")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe) spawns a child process — BlueHammer SYSTEM shell AIInstallation Medium
MsMpEng.exe effectively never spawns child processes during normal operation. A child of MsMpEng.exe (especially a shell or LOLBin) indicates the SYSTEM-privileged shell described as the BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) exploit outcome. Single-event, very-low-baseline detection of the privesc paying off into code execution as SYSTEM. Rationale: Uses the article's stated outcome — attackers 'spawn a SYSTEM-privileged shell' — expressed as the near-zero-baseline anomaly of MsMpEng.exe being a parent process. The Defender-helper allowlist (MpCmdRun/NisSrv/WerFault) keeps recall high while suppressing the only legitimate children. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-microsoft-defender-flaw-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks/ • https://www.penligent.ai/hackinglabs/bluehammer-redsun-and-the-windows-defender-race-to-system/ • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/windows-zero-day-bluehammer
ATT&CKT1068 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Defender helper launches (MpCmdRun.exe, NisSrv.exe) — excluded by allowlist
  • WerFault.exe / Windows Error Reporting spawned when MsMpEng crashes — excluded by allowlist
  • Third-party EDR/AV instrumentation that re-parents or hooks MsMpEng, mislabeling the parent image
  • Defender platform upgrade transiently relaunching engine components
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("MpCmdRun.exe", "NisSrv.exe", "MpCopyAccelerator.exe", "MsMpEngCP.exe", "WerFault.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child's FileName, full command line and integrity level — a System-integrity cmd.exe/powershell.exe or LOLBin child of MsMpEng is a confirmed hit; benign reasons are limited to the allowlisted helpers. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (attacker has SYSTEM), kill the child process tree, and preserve memory/volatile data. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC2 (MsMpEng writing to System32) on the same host, enumerate actions taken under SYSTEM — new local accounts, SAM/registry hive access, service creation, shadow-copy deletion — and check for lateral movement from this host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("MpCmdRun.exe", "NisSrv.exe", "MpCopyAccelerator.exe", "MsMpEngCP.exe", "WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, ProcessTokenElevation, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\MsMpEng.exe"
| where NewProcessName !endswith @"\MpCmdRun.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith @"\NisSrv.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith @"\WerFault.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith @"\MpCopyAccelerator.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537") or SHA1 in~ ("72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537") or MD5 in~ ("72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537") or SHA1 in~ ("72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537") or MD5 in~ ("72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["72d67a6c1829e4b675992755edc59c24", "0cb6948805f797bf2a82807973b89537"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Convince an AI browser that it is playing a game, and it can hand over your login details. That is the finding behind&nbsp;BioShocking, a technique from security firm LayerX that tricked six AI browsers and assistants into copying a user's credentials and sending them to an attacker. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-

Progress Kemp LoadMaster Flaw Could Let Attackers Run Root Commands Pre-Auth

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A critical vulnerability in Progress Kemp LoadMaster can let an unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary commands as root on the appliance by sending a crafted request to its API. The flaw, tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-8037, carries a CVSS score of&nbsp;9.8 according to ZDI. A patch is available. If you run LoadMaster with the API enabled, update now. Progress&nbsp;published its advisory on June

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-33691 WAF bypass via whitespace-padded upload filename extension · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 pre-auth RCE via /accessv2 heap-overflow command injection · [LLM] Root command execution on Kemp LoadMaster appliance following /accessv2 exploitation · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
