Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 pre-auth RCE via /accessv2 heap-overflow command injection AIExploitation High
Hunts the watchTowr PoC payload shape for CVE-2026-8037: an unauthenticated POST to the LoadMaster /accessv2 API endpoint whose JSON body sprays many extra keys (g0..g60) each carrying a '; <cmd> # shell-injection string plus a 16-byte 'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' padding prefix and an apiuser value of four single quotes. This is the exact initial-access signature against an internet-facing appliance, not a generic web-attack template. Rationale: Grounded on the exact watchTowr PoC strings cross-checked from the labs.watchtowr.com write-up: endpoint /accessv2, the 16-byte 'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' heap-padding prefix, the '; cat /etc/passwd # injection, the g0..g60 key spray, and apiuser ''''. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because LoadMaster is a closed Kemp appliance not enrolled in EDR/XDR or AWS; the request body lives in WAF/proxy CEF or the appliance's own syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/enterprise-tech-in-shell-out-progress-kemp-loadmaster-uninitialized-heap-to-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-8037/ • https://community.progress.com/s/article/LoadMaster-Critical-Security-Bulletin-June-2026-CVE-2026-8037-CVE-2026-33691 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or watchTowr 'Detection Artefact' validation firing the same payload
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) sending CVE-2026-8037 check payloads to /accessv2
  • Internal red-team exercises replaying the public PoC
  • WAF in blocking mode logging the attempt as 'denied' (true positive but already mitigated)
  • Legitimate high-volume API credential validation traffic tripping the 20-POST burst threshold during automation onboarding
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "denied" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ips_reference_table>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the matching CommonSecurityLog rows; confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and the body contains the injection markers (g0..g60 spray, '; ... #, /etc/passwd). Check whether the WAF action was 'allowed' vs 'blocked'. 2) CONTAIN: If allowed, treat the LoadMaster as compromised at root — isolate it from the management network, block the source IP at the edge, and disable the LoadMaster API if not strictly required (per advisory). Begin emergency patch to GA v7.2.63.2 / LTSF v7.2.54.18. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the appliance's syslog (UC: root command execution) for shell activity (/etc/passwd reads, reverse shells), review LoadMaster config and SSH authorized_keys for persistence, and scope all source IPs that hit /accessv2 with these markers across the full retention window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/accessv2"
| where Message has_any ("'; cat /etc/passwd #", "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA", "/etc/passwd", "\"g60\"", "\"apiuser\":\"''''\"")
   or RequestContext has_any ("'; cat /etc/passwd #", "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA", "/etc/passwd")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Progress Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 Pre-Auth RCE Exploitation Attempt

Root command execution on Kemp LoadMaster appliance following /accessv2 exploitation AIExploitation Medium
Execution-phase confirmation for CVE-2026-8037: the injected command runs as root on the LoadMaster appliance. Hunts the appliance's forwarded syslog for shell-command execution indicators (/etc/passwd reads, /bin/sh -c, reverse-shell /dev/tcp/ or bash -i) originating from a host named like a LoadMaster, which should never legitimately spawn arbitrary shells. Rationale: Targets the article's core claim that the command 'runs as root' on the appliance. A load balancer spawning /bin/sh, reading /etc/passwd, or opening a /dev/tcp reverse shell is never legitimate, making these high-fidelity post-exploitation indicators. Empty Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch: the appliance cannot host an EDR agent — only its remote syslog is observable. Hunting tier because it depends on the appliance being configured to forward syslog and named per convention. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/enterprise-tech-in-shell-out-progress-kemp-loadmaster-uninitialized-heap-to-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-8037/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kemp support/diagnostic sessions where an admin legitimately opens a root shell for troubleshooting
  • Firmware update or backup routines that touch /etc/passwd or spawn shell helpers
  • Authorized configuration scripts run by the appliance's own automation
  • Penetration test PoC replay reading /etc/passwd
  • Syslog from a non-appliance host that happens to match the 'kemp'/'loadmaster' name substring
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "kemp-support" and SeverityLevel != "debug"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source host is genuinely the LoadMaster appliance and that the shell activity has no matching authorized admin/maintenance window; correlate the timestamp against /accessv2 POST hits (UC1) within the preceding minutes. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, isolate the appliance from management and production networks, capture a config/state snapshot for forensics, and rotate any credentials/keys stored on or reachable from the appliance. 3) HUNT: Enumerate persistence — SSH authorized_keys under /root, cron/systemd entries, modified LoadMaster config — and review egress firewall logs for outbound connections initiated by the appliance IP (reverse shell / tooling download).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Computer has_any ("loadmaster", "lmos", "kemp") or HostName has_any ("loadmaster", "lmos", "kemp")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/dev/tcp/", "bash -i", "/bin/sh -c", "/bin/bash -c", "; cat ", "| sh")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, SeverityLevel, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@host.name:(*loadmaster* OR *LoadMaster* OR *lmos* OR *kemp* OR *Kemp*)) AND ("/etc/passwd" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "bash -i" OR "/bin/sh -c" OR "/bin/bash -c")
WEB
index=* sourcetype=syslog (host=*loadmaster* OR host=*lmos* OR host=*kemp*) ("/etc/passwd" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "bash -i" OR "/bin/sh -c" OR "/bin/bash -c")
| table _time host process syslog_message
| sort - _time
| comment("LoadMaster forwards to a non-CIM syslog sourcetype; raw search. Scope host to your appliance naming convention.")
Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-33691 WAF bypass via whitespace-padded upload filename extension AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the second patched flaw in the same advisory: a WAF/upload extension-check bypass where whitespace padding around a filename extension (e.g. evil.php<space> or evil .php / %20.php) slips a disallowed file type past the filter. Detects upload requests to LoadMaster whose filename contains whitespace adjacent to an executable/script extension. Rationale: Grounded on the advisory's description of CVE-2026-33691 — 'whitespace padding in filenames could circumvent file upload extension checks.' Matches whitespace immediately adjacent to a script/executable extension in the upload filename or URL-encoded path, a pattern legitimate uploads almost never produce. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: appliance upload telemetry lives only in the front-end WAF/proxy, not in endpoint EDR or AWS. Cross-checked against: • https://community.progress.com/s/article/LoadMaster-Critical-Security-Bulletin-June-2026-CVE-2026-8037-CVE-2026-33691 • https://securityonline.info/kemp-loadmaster-vulnerabilities-waf-bypass-os-injection/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user uploading a legitimately named file that happens to contain a trailing space before a known extension
  • Document-management workflows that rename files with padded extensions
  • Automated tooling that URL-encodes spaces (%20) in legitimate filenames
  • Security scanner testing upload filters with whitespace mutation payloads
  • Double-extension business files (e.g. report.tar .gz) tripping the regex
Suppression filter
| where FileName !endswith " .gz" and FileName !endswith " .bz2" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ips_reference_table>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the captured filename and upload endpoint; confirm the whitespace is adjacent to an executable/script extension (.php/.cgi/.sh) rather than a benign document type, and identify the resulting stored path. 2) CONTAIN: If a script/webshell-capable file was accepted, quarantine it on the appliance, block the source IP, and confirm the appliance is patched to GA v7.2.63.2 / LTSF v7.2.54.18. 3) HUNT: Search appliance syslog for subsequent execution of the uploaded path, review web logs for requests back to the uploaded filename (webshell interaction), and scope all sources that submitted whitespace-padded upload filenames.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or RequestMethod =~ "PUT" or isempty(RequestMethod)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\s+\.(php|cgi|sh|pl|jsp|asp|aspx|exe)\b"
    or FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|cgi|sh|pl|jsp|asp|aspx|exe)\s+$"
    or RequestURL has_any ("%20.php", "%20.cgi", "%20.sh", ".php%20", ".cgi%20")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, FileName, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposure: internet-facing Oracle EBS Payments 12.2.3-12.2.15 unpatched for CVE-2026-46817 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound connections from Oracle EBS CVE-2026-46817 actor IP 45.84.137.125 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Oracle EBS iPayment ibytransmit path-traversal exploit (CVE-2026-46817) reading /etc/passwd · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Oracle EBS iPayment ibytransmit path-traversal exploit (CVE-2026-46817) reading /etc/passwd AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the Oracle iPayment file-transmission endpoint /OA_HTML/ibytransmit carrying the CODEX_PULL / FULL_FILE_PATH path-traversal payload used to exfiltrate /etc/passwd. This is the exact in-the-wild exploitation pattern for CVE-2026-46817 captured on Defused Cyber honeypots, not a generic web-exploit template. Rationale: Anchors on the obscure Oracle iPayment endpoint /OA_HTML/ibytransmit plus the CODEX_PULL/FULL_FILE_PATH/etc-passwd payload strings confirmed across BleepingComputer, Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and Rescana write-ups of the same honeypot capture — this endpoint sees near-zero legitimate external POST traffic, making it high-fidelity. Defender KQL left empty: Defender XDR does not ingest inbound HTTP request URIs/bodies for server processes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/oracle-payments-cve-2026-46817-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/exploitation-of-recent-oracle-e-business-suite-vulnerability-begins/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-critical-oracle-e-business-suite-cve-2026-46817-vulnerability-targeting-oracle-payments-module
ATT&CKT1190 T1003.008 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate B2B payment partner integrations that genuinely use the iPayment ibytransmit file-transmission interface
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Nessus, Qualys) probing the EBS endpoint during scheduled scans
  • Internal red-team / pentest validation of CVE-2026-46817
  • Oracle support or DBA diagnostics hitting the endpoint from a known jump host
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Tenable")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matched event and check whether the XML body contains CODEX_PULL with FULL_FILE_PATH=/etc/passwd, and whether HttpStatusCode == 200 (successful file read). Reputation-check the SrcIpAddr (45.84.137.125 / AS136787 PacketHub is the known actor). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and, if a 200 with file-read payload is confirmed, isolate the EBS web tier and rotate any OS/app credentials exposed via /etc/passwd-adjacent reads. 3) Hunt: review web logs for other POSTs to /OA_HTML/* from the same IP, look for webshell drops in the OA_HTML doc root, and check for new outbound connections or interactive shells from the EBS host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/OA_HTML/ibytransmit"
| extend PayloadHit = Url has_any ("CODEX_PULL","FULL_FILE_PATH","/etc/passwd","DeliveryRequest")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, PayloadHit
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound connections from Oracle EBS CVE-2026-46817 actor IP 45.84.137.125 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts any network connection from the confirmed CVE-2026-46817 exploitation source IP 45.84.137.125 (AS136787 PacketHub, France) to internet-facing Oracle E-Business Suite hosts on 443. A pure IOC pivot that catches the actor even when WAF/web-log payload telemetry is missing. Rationale: 45.84.137.125 is the single confirmed actor IP from the Defused honeypot capture, cross-validated by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; an external IP-only match against EBS hosts is low-volume and high-fidelity for this specific campaign. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: the EBS web tier is a Linux server whose firewall/flow telemetry does not map to the standard Datadog or CloudWatch sources in scope. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.securityweek.com/exploitation-of-recent-oracle-e-business-suite-vulnerability-begins/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-critical-oracle-e-business-suite-cve-2026-46817-vulnerability-targeting-oracle-payments-module

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed validation / sandbox detonation traffic sourced from the same hosting range
  • Security researcher or scanner sharing the AS136787 PacketHub egress range
  • Stale NAT/proxy reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant
  • An analyst manually curl-testing the IOC from a corporate egress that the IP happens to also use
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DstHostname/DeviceName is an internet-facing Oracle EBS host and correlate the connection time with any /OA_HTML/ibytransmit POSTs in web logs. 2) Contain: block 45.84.137.125 (and consider the AS136787 PacketHub range) at the perimeter firewall and WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination host for successful 200 responses on iPayment endpoints, new files in the OA_HTML doc root, and any outbound beaconing from the EBS host post-connection.

Exposure: internet-facing Oracle EBS Payments 12.2.3-12.2.15 unpatched for CVE-2026-46817 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces Oracle E-Business Suite hosts carrying CVE-2026-46817 (Oracle Payments, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15) so the SOC can prioritise the May 2026 CSPU patch on internet-facing instances before opportunistic exploitation. Exposure-reduction hunt tied to the actively exploited CVE. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-46817) and affected version band (12.2.3-12.2.15) named by NVD/The Hacker News and confirmed actively exploited; joining TVM to IsInternetFacing prioritises the exact hosts the actor can reach. Sigma omitted (posture/exposure query, not a single-event detection); Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted (no vulnerability-inventory event in those schemas). Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46817 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-cve-2026.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/oracle-payments-cve-2026-46817-exploitation/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EBS hosts already patched with the May 2026 CSPU but pending a TVM rescan (stale inventory)
  • Internal-only EBS instances flagged as exposure but not actually reachable from the internet
  • Decommissioned/test EBS servers still reporting to TVM
  • Version banner mismatch where a compensating WAF virtual-patch is already in place
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort results by IsInternetFacing and confirm each host's actual internet reachability and current EBS patch level against the May 2026 CSPU. 2) Contain: virtual-patch internet-facing unpatched hosts at the WAF (block /OA_HTML/ibytransmit) and schedule emergency patching. 3) Hunt: for any host that was internet-facing and unpatched during the exploitation window, retro-hunt web logs for /OA_HTML/ibytransmit POSTs and connections from 45.84.137.125.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Internet-facing Oracle PeopleSoft exposed/exploited via CVE-2026-35273 PSEMHUB SSRF (ShinyHunters) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces internet-facing PeopleSoft hosts carrying CVE-2026-35273 and anomalous access to the Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) servlet — the unauthenticated SSRF→RCE entry point ShinyHunters/UNC6240 exploited as a zero-day between May 27 and June 9 2026. Pairs vulnerability exposure with the specific exploited endpoint so SOC can prioritise the actual attack surface, not a generic CVE list. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploited component (PSEMHUB / Environment Management Hub) and the exact CVE id CVE-2026-35273 (CVSS 9.8 unauth SSRF→RCE), not a generic web-exploit template. PSEMHUB is an internal hub rarely reached externally, so external hits are high-fidelity. Defender path is vuln-exposure, Sentinel path is the exploit endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2026-35273.html • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-active-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-cve-2026-35273/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub agents (PSEMAgent) checking in to PSEMHUB from internal app/batch servers
  • Internal Oracle/PeopleSoft admins browsing PSEMHUB during environment configuration
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing PSEMHUB and PSIGW paths
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting the PeopleSoft web tier
  • PeopleSoft Integration Broker (PSIGW) normal SOAP traffic from trusted partners
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168." and cIP !startswith "172.16."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the hitting cIP is external/untrusted and whether the PeopleTools version (8.61/8.62/8.63) is unpatched for CVE-2026-35273; review PSEMHUB request bodies/user-agents for SSRF markers. 2) Contain: apply Oracle's emergency mitigation/patch, restrict PSEMHUB and PSIGW to internal/management networks via WAF/ACL, and snapshot the host for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host — look for java-spawned shells, MeshCentral/node.exe, and outbound to azurenetfiles.net or 142.11.200.184/29.

| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(csMethod), Statuses=make_set(scStatus), TotalRespBytes=sum(scBytes), Clients=make_set(cIP, 50) by Computer, csUriStem, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

Oracle PeopleSoft Java/app-server process spawning shell or recon binary (CVE-2026-35273 post-exploit) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the PeopleSoft web/app tier (WebLogic java.exe, psae.exe, PSEMAgent.exe, psadmin.exe) spawning command shells, LOLBins, node.exe, or AD-recon utilities — the hands-on-keyboard activity Mandiant observed after CVE-2026-35273 RCE (internal PeopleSoft recon, lateral-movement scripts, MeshCentral install). A PeopleSoft Java process spawning cmd/powershell is abnormal and indicates code execution through the exploited servlet. Rationale: Article-specific because the parent set is the PeopleSoft web/app tier and the child set mirrors Mandiant's reported post-exploit behaviour (internal PeopleSoft recon, lateral-movement scripting, node.exe for MeshCentral). A Java/PeopleTools process spawning a shell is the textbook signal of the CVE-2026-35273 RCE being used. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit • https://www.securityweek.com/google-confirms-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-by-shinyhunters/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PeopleSoft Process Scheduler / App Engine (psae.exe) legitimately invoking cmd.exe wrappers for batch jobs
  • Admin/DevOps shell scripts launched from a Java-based management console
  • PeopleTools COBOL/SQR batch processing that shells out to net.exe for share access
  • Monitoring agents querying whoami/net during inventory collection
  • Application deployment automation running certutil for cert installs
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "psae.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PS_HOME","PRCSRQST","psprcs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for recon (whoami/nltest/net group), download (certutil/bitsadmin/curl), or MeshCentral (node.exe) strings, and confirm the host is a PeopleSoft server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and capture parent java.exe command line + loaded modules. 3) Hunt: check UC3 for outbound to azurenetfiles.net / 142.11.200.184/29, UC5 for the listed file hashes, and UC4 for .zst staging archives on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java.exe","psae.exe","PSEMAgent.exe","psadmin.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\PeopleSoft\", @"\pt8.6", @"\PT8.6")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","psae.exe","PSEMAgent.exe","psadmin.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Oracle PeopleSoft App Server Spawning Shell or Recon Binary (CVE-2026-35273)
id: 7c2e4b9a-1d83-4f6b-9c21-3a7e5f0d12ab
description: PeopleSoft web/app-tier Java or PeopleTools process spawning a command shell, LOLBin or AD-recon utility, consistent with post-exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by ShinyHunters/UNC6240.
references:
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nissan-discloses-employee-data-breach-linked-to-oracle-zero-day-attacks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\psae.exe'
      - '\PSEMAgent.exe'
      - '\psadmin.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\nltest.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\java.exe OR *\Java.exe OR *\psae.exe OR *\PSEMAgent.exe OR *\psadmin.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\net.exe OR *\nltest.exe OR *\certutil.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(java|psae|psemagent|psadmin)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|cscript|wscript|node|whoami|net|net1|nltest|certutil|bitsadmin|curl)\.exe$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("java.exe","psae.exe","PSEMAgent.exe","psadmin.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","node.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","nltest.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT user="*$" | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("java.exe","psae.exe","PSEMAgent.exe","psadmin.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","node.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","nltest.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT user="*$" | sort - lastTime
PeopleSoft host beaconing to ShinyHunters MeshCentral C2 (azurenetfiles.net / 142.11.200.184-29 / 176.120.22.24) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on DNS resolution of azurenetfiles.net and outbound sessions from internal hosts to ShinyHunters infrastructure: the MeshCentral C2 wss://azurenetfiles.net:443/agent.ashx, the staging IPs 142.11.200.186-190 (Python SimpleHTTP on 8888) and 176.120.22.24. Server segments should virtually never initiate this egress, making it high-fidelity for the CVE-2026-35273 data-theft campaign. Rationale: Every indicator is externally corroborated: azurenetfiles.net is the hardcoded MeshCentral C2 (wss://azurenetfiles.net:443/agent.ashx), 142.11.200.186-190 hosted attacker Python SimpleHTTP staging on port 8888, and the IPs shared a TLS cert CN of azurenetfiles.net. Server-tier egress to these is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4184408/oracle-peoplesoft-zero%E2%80%91day-fuels-shinyhunters-extortion-spree.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/EDR sandbox detonation or sinkhole infrastructure resolving azurenetfiles.net for research
  • Security team validating IOCs by intentionally connecting to the listed IPs
  • Proxy/secure-web-gateway logging the blocked connection (already-mitigated TP, not benign)
  • IP reuse: 176.120.22.24 or the 142.11.200.0/24 block reassigned to a benign tenant after takedown
  • Internal DNS resolver forwarding a downstream client's query (attribute to true source IP)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/host — if it is a PeopleSoft server or the InitiatingProcess is node.exe/java.exe, treat as confirmed C2; check for the MeshCentral agent.ashx URL. 2) Contain: block azurenetfiles.net and 142.11.200.184/29 + 176.120.22.24 at firewall/proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and terminate the MeshCentral/node process and its service. 3) Hunt: review UC4 for zstd staging archives, UC2 for the spawning java process, and pull all sessions to 142.11.200.184/29:8888 to scope exfiltrated data volume.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "azurenetfiles.net"
    or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "142.11.200.184/29")
    or RemoteIP == "176.120.22.24"
| extend MeshCentralC2 = (RemoteUrl has "agent.ashx" and RemoteUrl has "azurenetfiles.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, MeshCentralC2, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(
    ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Channel="DNS"
),
(
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == "176.120.22.24" or ipv4_is_in_range(DestinationIP, "142.11.200.184/29") or DestinationDnsDomain has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Host=SourceHostName, Indicator=strcat(DestinationIP, ":", tostring(DestinationPort)), Channel="Firewall"
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

zstd data-staging archives written on PeopleSoft host (ShinyHunters exfil prep) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects creation of zstd-compressed archives (.zst / .tar.zst) on server-tier hosts by PeopleSoft, node.exe (MeshCentral), shell or scripting processes — the compression method Mandiant observed ShinyHunters using to stage HR/payroll data for exfiltration after CVE-2026-35273. zstd archiving on a PeopleSoft application server is abnormal and immediately precedes egress to attacker staging servers. Rationale: zstd compression is the corroborated, distinctive staging TTP Mandiant tied to this campaign, and scoping the writer process to the PeopleSoft/MeshCentral tier separates it from generic compression. Sorting by file size surfaces the bulk HR/payroll archives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/google-confirms-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-by-shinyhunters/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1567 T1213
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup tooling that uses zstd compression (e.g. Borg, restic, PostgreSQL/MongoDB dumps with zstd)
  • Developers compressing logs or build artifacts with zstd on a server
  • Container image layer extraction writing .zst blobs
  • PeopleSoft log-rotation or data-export jobs that legitimately produce compressed archives
  • Filesystem replication/sync tools transferring pre-compressed .zst files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Veeam\", @"\restic", @"\borg", @"\Commvault\") or FolderPath has_any (@"\Backup\", @"\backups\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the .zst path, size, and parent command line — large archives in temp/web dirs written by node.exe/java.exe/psae.exe are suspect; confirm host is a PeopleSoft data store. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive for scoping which PII tables were collected, and block egress to UC3 destinations. 3) Hunt: correlate the file-write time to outbound sessions to 142.11.200.184/29:8888 (staging) and azurenetfiles.net, and check other PeopleSoft hosts for the same .zst pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".zst" or FileName endswith ".tar.zst"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("zstd.exe","zstd","node.exe","java.exe","psae.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh","python.exe","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".zst"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("zstd","node.exe","java.exe","psae.exe","powershell","pwsh","cmd.exe","bash","sh","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TargetFileSize desc

Known ShinyHunters PeopleSoft payload/staging file hashes on disk (CVE-2026-35273) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any of the five SHA256 hashes tied to the CVE-2026-35273 PeopleSoft intrusions appearing in file-write or process-execution telemetry. Pure IOC match for the campaign's dropped web shells/staging tooling, giving an immediate high-confidence hit on affected hosts. Rationale: Direct SHA256 IOC match against the five campaign hashes from the article's IOC set; hash hits are unambiguous and warrant alerting tier. Union of file-write and process-exec catches both the drop and any subsequent execution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nissan-discloses-employee-data-breach-linked-to-oracle-zero-day-attacks/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-active-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-cve-2026-35273/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hash collision is cryptographically negligible — near-zero benign FP
  • Security team intentionally placing the IOC sample on a sandbox/analysis host
  • EDR quarantine copies of the file re-triggering the file-write detection
  • Backup/AV scan re-reading the quarantined sample
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Quarantine", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\VirusShare", @"\Malware\Samples\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit and capture the file path/host; if on a PeopleSoft server, treat as confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, terminate any running instance, and preserve memory/disk for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for all five hashes, then pivot to UC2 (java→shell), UC3 (azurenetfiles.net / staging-IP C2), and UC4 (.zst archives) on every host that matched.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious Chromium-based extension that spoofs the AI-powered answer engine Perplexity AI redirects browser search traffic using MV3 APIs and intermediary infrastructure. The post Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online AICommand & Control High
Hunts browser connections/DNS resolutions to the attacker-controlled search-interception infrastructure (perplexity-ai.online and related oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) used by the fake 'Search for perplexity ai' Chromium extension. Because the extension routes every Omnibox query and keystroke-level suggestion through this domain before redirecting to a real engine, any browser-originated traffic to these hosts is high-fidelity evidence of an infected endpoint. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interception domain perplexity-ai.online (confirmed by both the MSFT blog and The Hacker News) plus the pre-extracted secondary infra oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws, scoped to browser parent processes — a typosquat domain reached by a browser is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst detonating the extension sample in a managed sandbox host
  • Web proxy / secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or URL-categorizing the domain on a user's behalf
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS-sinkhole tooling resolving the IOC for blocking
  • A user who clicked the lookalike landing page once but did not install (single browse vs. repeated query routing)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which device/user generated the traffic and whether the 'Search for perplexity ai' extension (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) is installed; check if default search provider was overridden to perplexity-ai.online. 2) Contain: force-remove the extension via browser policy/ExtensionInstallBlocklist, reset the default search engine, and block perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on all other hosts resolving these domains and review browsing/search history routed through the domain for sensitive query exposure during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to Perplexity Typosquat Search-Interception Domain
id: 5b3e9a42-7c1f-4d2a-9f6e-2a1c8d4b7e90
description: Detects DNS resolution of perplexity-ai.online and related infrastructure used by a malicious Chromium extension spoofing Perplexity AI to intercept browser search queries.

detection:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*perplexity-ai.online* OR *oda.digital* OR extension.tilda.ws)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(perplexity-ai\.online|oda\.digital|extension\.tilda\.ws)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" OR DNS.query="*oda.digital*" OR DNS.query="extension.tilda.ws") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" OR DNS.query="*oda.digital*" OR DNS.query="extension.tilda.ws") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts for the unique Chrome Web Store extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd ('Search for perplexity ai') appearing in browser extension folder paths or written files on managed endpoints. The extension ID is a globally unique 32-char identifier, so any file-system artifact bearing it is a deterministic indicator that the taken-down malicious search hijacker was installed. Rationale: The 32-char extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd is a globally unique store identifier (confirmed via the Chrome Web Store and crx4chrome listings), so its presence in any extension folder path is a deterministic install indicator with effectively no collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1176 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup software capturing the Chrome 'User Data' profile directory that still contains the extension folder
  • IR/forensic collection tooling copying browser profiles for offline analysis
  • AV/EDR scanning or quarantining the extension folder (file-access touches the path)
  • Sync of an already-infected profile to a new device via Chrome profile sync before takedown
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ActionType (FileCreated = fresh install vs FileDeleted = remediation) and identify the user profile and browser hosting the extension folder. 2) Contain: remove the extension, push it to the browser ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy, and reset the hijacked default search provider; block perplexity-ai.online at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 network telemetry to confirm queries were exfiltrated, and sweep the fleet for the same extension ID to find all installs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
